uni-common-eng-graphics.title: Engineering Graphics (First Year)
uni-common-eng-graphics.description: Full B.Tech Engineering Graphics (First Year) syllabus: Drawing Fundamentals, Scales & Conics. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Drawing Fundamentals, Scales & Conics
courses.summary: Drawing sheets, line types, lettering, dimensioning, scales and the conic sections: the foundation of every engineering drawing. Covers topics commonly taught in first-year B.Tech Engineering Graphics courses.
outcomes: Learners can choose sheet sizes and line types per BIS conventions
Learners can dimension a drawing without redundancy
Learners can compute the representative fraction and plain-scale length
Learners can locate vertices of ellipse, parabola and hyperbola from eccentricity

scenes.text: Kabir submits his first drawing on a random sheet with all lines equally dark.
His instructor says: 'A drawing is a language. Line type is its grammar.'

steps.title: Standard sheets
steps.body:
Drawing sheets follow the ISO A-series (also adopted by BIS). The A0 sheet has area 1 m² and size **841 × 1189 mm**. Each next size halves the longer side: A1 = 594 × 841, A2 = 420 × 594, A3 = 297 × 420, **A4 = 210 × 297 mm**. The aspect ratio is 1 : √2 for every size.

A drawing sheet has a border (usually 10 mm, or 20 mm on the binding side) and a **title block** at the bottom right giving title, scale, projection symbol, name and date.

steps.title: Types of lines
steps.body:
- **Continuous thick**: visible outlines and edges.
- **Continuous thin**: dimension lines, extension lines, projection lines, hatching.
- **Dashed (medium)**: hidden edges.
- **Chain thin (long dash–dot)**: centre lines, axes of symmetry, pitch circles.
- **Chain thick at ends**: cutting-plane lines.
- **Continuous thin freehand / zig-zag**: short break lines.

Pencil grades: H or 2H for construction and thin lines, HB for thick lines and lettering.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · A-series sizes
steps.body:
Find the area of A3 in m².
- Step 1: A3 = 297 × 420 mm = 124 740 mm².
- Step 2: convert: 124 740 / 10⁶ = **0.1247 m²**.
- Check: A0 = 1 m², and A3 is A0 halved three times, so 1/8 = 0.125 m² ✓.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Sheets from A0
steps.body:
How many A4 sheets fit in one A0?
- Each step down halves the area: A0→A1→A2→A3→A4 is 4 halvings.
- 2⁴ = **16 sheets**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using thick lines for dimension lines.
- Drawing centre lines as plain continuous lines.
- Lettering in mixed heights; standard heights are 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10 mm and so on, with strokes of uniform thickness.

quiz.why: Hidden detail is shown by dashed lines of medium thickness.

quiz.why: A0 to A2 is two halvings, so 2² = 4 sheets.

story.title: The shaft that was machined twice

scenes.text: A drawing of a shaft gives the length as a chain of three dimensions plus an overall length.
The machinist finds they disagree by 0.5 mm and scraps the part. Redundant dimensions cause ambiguity.

steps.title: Elements of a dimension
steps.body:
A dimension has **extension lines** (thin, extend 1–2 mm beyond the arrowhead, with a small gap from the object), a **dimension line** with arrowheads (thin, about 3 mm long, 1:3 width-to-length), the **figure** (above the line, readable from the bottom or the right), and symbols such as Ø for diameter, R for radius, □ for square.

Two systems of placing figures: **aligned** and **unidirectional**.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Dimension each feature once only; never repeat.
- Place dimensions outside the view where possible and avoid crossing dimension lines.
- Put the smaller dimension nearer to the object.
- Never use a centre line or an outline as a dimension line.
- Methods: chain, parallel (baseline), combined. Parallel dimensioning avoids accumulated tolerance error.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Redundancy
steps.body:
A bar is 100 mm long and has three segments 30, 30 and 30 mm, with overall 100 mm also given.
- Sum of parts = 90 mm ≠ 100 mm → the drawing is over-dimensioned and contradictory.
- Fix: omit one segment (or the overall) or bracket one as a reference dimension, e.g. (40).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Angular and radial
steps.body:
A circular flange has a pitch circle diameter (PCD) of 80 mm and six equally spaced holes.
- Angular spacing = 360° / 6 = **60°**.
- Chord between adjacent hole centres = PCD × sin(30°) = 80 × 0.5 = **40 mm** (equals the radius, because a regular hexagon has side = radius).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the diameter symbol in front of a radius.
- Ending dimension lines in open arrowheads of different sizes in one drawing.
- Dimensioning to hidden lines.

activity.prompt: A flange has 8 equally spaced holes. What is the angle between adjacent holes (degrees)?

quiz.q: Which symbol precedes the figure for a diameter?
quiz.why: Ø denotes diameter, R radius and □ a square section.
Dimension and extension lines are thin continuous lines.

quiz.q: Which method avoids accumulation of tolerance?
quiz.why: Each feature is measured from one datum in the parallel method, so errors do not add.

scenes.text: An architect must draw a 24 m hall on a sheet 420 mm wide.
She picks a scale of 1:100, so 24 m becomes 240 mm.

steps.title: Representative fraction
steps.body:
**RF = length of the drawing / actual length of the object** (both in the same unit).

RF = 1 is full size, RF < 1 is **reduction** (e.g. 1:50), RF > 1 is **enlargement** (e.g. 5:1). Recommended scales (ISO 5455): reduction 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100; enlargement 2:1, 5:1, 10:1.

Types of scale: **plain**, **diagonal** (reads a third unit), **vernier**, **comparative** and **scale of chords**. The **length of scale** = RF × maximum length to be measured.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · RF and plain scale length
steps.body:
A scale shows 1 cm for 5 m; draw a plain scale to read up to 60 m.
- Step 1: 5 m = 500 cm, so RF = 1/500.
- Step 2: length of scale = RF × 60 m = 6000 cm / 500 = **12 cm**.
- Step 3: divide 12 cm into 12 equal main divisions of 1 cm each (5 m); subdivide the first into 5 parts of 1 m each.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Diagonal scale
steps.body:
Diagonal scale 1:40 to read metres, decimetres and centimetres, up to 6 m.
- Length of scale = 6 m / 40 = 6000 mm / 40 = **150 mm**.
- 150 mm is divided into 6 main parts of 25 mm (1 m each); the left part is divided into 10 parts (1 dm each).
- Draw 10 horizontal lines of equal spacing; diagonals from the top left corner to the base of the first subdivision give 1 cm reading per horizontal level.
- Least count = 1 m / (10 × 10) = **0.01 m = 1 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing units in RF (cm in the numerator, m in the denominator).
- Reading the scale from the wrong zero: the zero is at the end of the first main division, with the subdivisions to its left.
- Labelling the drawing with the scale it was drawn in, but then printing it at a different size. Use a graphical bar scale if printing may change.

story.title: Why a torch beam draws curves on a wall

scenes.text: Tilting a torch changes the lit shape on a wall from a circle to an ellipse, then an open curve.
These are the conic sections, cut from a cone by planes at different angles.

steps.title: Eccentricity method
steps.body:
A conic is the locus of a point P that moves so that **distance from a fixed point (focus) / distance from a fixed straight line (directrix) = e** (constant eccentricity).

- e < 1: **ellipse**
- e = 1: **parabola**
- e > 1: **hyperbola**

The vertex V lies on the axis (perpendicular from the focus to the directrix) where VF/VD = e. If the focus-to-directrix distance is d, then **VD = d/(1+e)** and VF = e·d/(1+e).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Ellipse construction
steps.body:
Focus is 50 mm from the directrix and e = 2/3.
- Step 1: divide the axis FD into 5 equal parts (2 + 3 = 5 units); VF = 2 parts = 20 mm and VD = 30 mm.
- Check: VF/VD = 20/30 = 2/3 ✓; formula VF = e d/(1+e) = (2/3)(50)/(5/3) = **20 mm**.
- Step 2: from V draw a perpendicular VE = VF; join D–E to get the e-line. Draw perpendiculars at points 1, 2, 3 on the axis meeting the e-line; with F as centre and radius equal to the perpendicular length, cut arcs on the corresponding perpendicular on both sides. Join smoothly.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Parabola and hyperbola vertices
steps.body:
Focus 40 mm from the directrix.
- Parabola (e = 1): VF = 40 × 1/2 = **20 mm** (vertex is midway).
- Hyperbola (e = 3/2): VF = 1.5 × 40 / 2.5 = **24 mm**, VD = 40/2.5 = 16 mm.
- Rectangular hyperbola has asymptotes at 90° and e = √2; it models Boyle's law P·V = constant.

steps.title: Real use
steps.body: Planetary orbits are ellipses; headlamp reflectors and satellite dishes are paraboloids; cooling-tower silhouettes are hyperbolae.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the focus as the centre of the ellipse; the focus is not the centre.
- Measuring the arc radius from the directrix instead of the focus.
- Freehand joining of points: use a french curve through all the points smoothly.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone · Plan a drawing sheet

scenes.text: You must draw a bracket 240 mm long, 120 mm wide, scale 1:2, in two views.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Plan first
steps.body:
Choose the scale, compute the sheet space the views need (plus space for dimensions, about 20 mm each side and 30 mm between views), then the sheet size.

At 1:2 the views are 120 mm × 60 mm. Two views side by side plus gaps: 120 + 30 + 60 + margins fit comfortably in A3 or A4 landscape (A4 landscape drawing area = 277 × 190 mm after 10 mm margins).

steps.title: Worked check
steps.body: Length 240 mm × 1/2 = 120 mm. Width 120 × 1/2 = 60 mm. Total horizontal need = 120 + 30 (gap) + 60 + 2×20 (dimension space) = **250 mm** ≤ 277 mm ✓, so A4 landscape works.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Picking a sheet before computing space, which leads to cramped dimensions or views drifting into the title block.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Force systems & equilibrium
courses.summary: Forces as vectors, resultants, Lami's theorem, moments and couples, free-body diagrams and support reactions of beams.
outcomes: Find the resultant of concurrent forces by components
Apply Lami's theorem and the equations of equilibrium
Compute moments, couples and the resultant of parallel forces
Draw free-body diagrams and find beam reactions

lessons.title: Forces as vectors and the resultant

scenes.text: Two tugboats pull a barge: one with 100 kN due east, another with 150 kN at 60° north of east.
The harbour master asks: what single pull would do the same job, and in which direction?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A **force** is a vector: magnitude, direction, point of application. Unit: newton (N) = kg·m/s². **Resultant** R is the single force equivalent to a system. Principle of transmissibility: a force may slide along its line of action without changing its external effect on a rigid body.

Parallelogram law: for forces P and Q with angle θ between them, **R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ)** and the angle α of R from P is **tan α = Q sin θ / (P + Q cos θ)**.

steps.title: Resolution into components
steps.body: A force F at angle θ to the x-axis has **Fx = F cos θ, Fy = F sin θ**. For many forces: **Rx = ΣFx, Ry = ΣFy, R = √(Rx²+Ry²), tan α = Ry/Rx**. Take care with the quadrant of α.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cos where sin is needed because the angle is measured from the vertical.
- Adding magnitudes instead of vectors.
- Using +2PQcosθ with the wrong θ: θ is the angle between the two forces drawn tail-to-tail.

activity.prompt: Two forces of 100 N and 150 N act at a point with 60° between them. Find the magnitude of the resultant (N).

quiz.why: R² = F²+F²+2F²cos120° = 2F² − F² = F².

quiz.why: External effect on a rigid body is unchanged when sliding along the line of action.

If Rx = −3 N and Ry = 4 N, R equals:
quiz.why: √(9+16) = 5 N (second quadrant).

quiz.q: Unit of force in SI is:
quiz.why: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

lessons.title: Equilibrium of a particle and Lami's theorem

scenes.text: A 1000 N signboard hangs from a knot where two cables meet, one at 30° and one at 45° to the horizontal.
Which cable carries more load?

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
A particle is in equilibrium when the resultant is zero: **ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0** (planar). For three concurrent forces, **Lami's theorem**: each force is proportional to the sine of the angle between the other two:
**F1/sin α = F2/sin β = F3/sin γ**, where α is the angle between F2 and F3, etc.

steps.title: Solved example – signboard
steps.body:
Let T1 (30°) and T2 (45°) act on the knot on opposite sides, W = 1000 N downward.
- ΣFx: T1 cos30° = T2 cos45° → T2 = 1.2247 T1
- ΣFy: T1 sin30° + T2 sin45° = 1000 → T1(0.5 + 0.8660) = 1000
- **T1 = 732.1 N**, **T2 = 896.6 N**
Check: vertical = 366.0 + 634.0 = 1000 ✓. The 45° cable is more loaded.

steps.title: Lami example
steps.body: A 200 N weight hangs from two strings with 90° between them, symmetric. Angle between W and each string = 135°. T1/sin135° = 200/sin90° → **T1 = 141.4 N** (same for T2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Lami needs exactly **three** concurrent forces.
- Using the angle with the horizontal instead of the angle *between the other two forces*.
- Not checking the answer by substituting into the second equation.

lessons.title: Moment of a force, Varignon's theorem and couples

scenes.text: A mechanic cannot loosen a nut with a 0.2 m spanner but succeeds when he slides a 1 m pipe over the handle.
Same push, longer arm, larger turning effect: that is moment.

steps.title: Moment
steps.body:
**Moment of force F about point O = F × d** (d = perpendicular distance from O to the line of action). Unit N·m; counter-clockwise is usually positive. In vector form M = r × F.

**Varignon's theorem:** the moment of a force about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components about that point.

steps.title: Couples
steps.body: A **couple** is two equal, opposite, parallel forces with different lines of action. Net force = 0, moment = **F × d** (arm d), the same about every point – a free vector. A force F at A can be replaced by the same force at O plus a couple F·d (force–couple system).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. 200 N perpendicular to a 0.6 m spanner: M = 200×0.6 = **120 N·m**.
2. 100 N at 30° to a beam, applied 3 m from the support: M = 100 sin30° × 3 = **150 N·m** (only the perpendicular component turns).
3. Couple: two 50 N forces 0.4 m apart: **20 N·m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the length of the arm instead of the *perpendicular* distance.
- Sign errors: pick a convention at the start and keep it.
- Treating a couple as having a position – it does not.

steps.title: Supports and FBD
steps.body:
Draw the body alone, then all external forces and reactions.
- **Roller**: 1 reaction, perpendicular to the surface.
- **Hinge/pin**: 2 reactions (Rx, Ry).
- **Fixed (cantilever)**: Rx, Ry and a moment M.

Planar equilibrium: **ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0**. A UDL of w (kN/m) over length L acts as W = wL at the middle of its length.

steps.title: Solved example 1 – simply supported beam
steps.body:
L = 6 m, point load 12 kN at 2 m from A, UDL 4 kN/m over the whole span (total 24 kN at 3 m).
- ΣM about A: RB×6 = 12×2 + 24×3 = 96 → **RB = 16 kN**
- ΣFy: RA = 12 + 24 − 16 = **20 kN**

steps.title: Solved example 2 – cantilever
steps.body: 3 m cantilever, 5 kN at the tip, UDL 2 kN/m (6 kN at 1.5 m). Reaction R = 5 + 6 = **11 kN**; fixed-end moment M = 5×3 + 6×1.5 = **24 kN·m**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the UDL resultant acts at its centroid.
- Wrong reaction directions on rollers.
- Not verifying with ΣM about the other support.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: For parallel forces: **R = ΣF** (with signs) and **R·x̄ = ΣF·x** (Varignon). If R = 0 but ΣM ≠ 0 the system reduces to a couple.

steps.title: Worked
steps.body: Take downward positive: R = −10 + 20 + 30 = 40 N down. Moments about O: 20×2 + 30×5 = 190 N·m. x̄ = 190/40 = **4.75 m** from O.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Always verify by taking moments about a second point; the resultant must produce the same moment about every point.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Centroid, centre of gravity & moment of inertia
courses.summary: First moments and centroids of lines, areas and composites, theorems of Pappus, second moments of area, parallel and perpendicular axis theorems, radius of gyration.

lessons.title: Centroid and first moment of area

scenes.text: A workshop technician cuts a steel plate into a semicircle and wants to balance it on a pin.
Where must the pin go? That point is the centroid.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **First moment of area** about an axis: Q = ∫y dA. **Centroid** (x̄, ȳ): **x̄ = ∫x dA / A, ȳ = ∫y dA / A**. For a body of uniform density and thickness the centre of gravity coincides with the centroid. An axis of symmetry always contains the centroid; the first moment about a centroidal axis is zero.

steps.title: Standard results
steps.body:
- Rectangle b×h: ȳ = h/2 from base.
- Triangle: ȳ = h/3 from base.
- Semicircle radius R: ȳ = **4R/3π** from the diameter.
- Quarter circle: x̄ = ȳ = 4R/3π.
- Circular sector (half angle α rad): x̄ = (2R sin α)/(3α) from the centre.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Semicircle R = 60 mm: ȳ = 4×60/(3π) = 240/9.4248 = **25.46 mm** above the diameter.

steps.title: Solved example 2 – by integration
steps.body: Triangle with base b, height h; strip of width b(1 − y/h) at height y: ∫y dA = ∫₀ʰ y·b(1−y/h) dy = b(h²/2 − h²/3) = bh²/6. A = bh/2 → **ȳ = h/3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Measuring 4R/3π from the arc rather than from the diameter.
- Using h/2 for a triangle.
- Forgetting that x̄ and ȳ must be measured from the same stated origin.

quiz.why: Medians meet at one-third height.

scenes.text: A fabricator welds a 100×20 mm flange on a 20×100 mm web to make a T-beam.
The designer needs the neutral axis position: the centroid from the bottom.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Split into simple shapes. **ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ / ΣAᵢ**, **x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ / ΣAᵢ**. Holes are negative areas.

steps.title: Solved example 1 – T-section
steps.body:
Flange 100×20 (top): A₁ = 2000 mm², y₁ = 110 from bottom. Web 20×100: A₂ = 2000, y₂ = 50.
ȳ = (2000×110 + 2000×50)/4000 = **80 mm** from the bottom.

steps.title: Second moment of area

scenes.text: A civil engineer looks at the triangular pattern of a railway bridge and asks why every panel is a triangle.
A triangle cannot change shape without changing a side length: it is rigid.

steps.title: Assumptions of the ideal truss
steps.body:
1. Members are straight and joined by frictionless pins.
2. Loads act only at joints.
3. Self-weight is neglected (or lumped at joints).

Therefore each member is a **two-force member**: axial tension or compression only, no bending.

steps.title: Perfect truss
steps.body: For j joints and m members, a simple plane truss is **perfect (just stiff)** when **m = 2j − 3**. If m < 2j − 3 it is a deficient (unstable) truss; if m > 2j − 3 it is redundant (statically indeterminate). With reactions r, the general count is m + r = 2j.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Triangle: j = 3, m = 3 → 2(3) − 3 = 3 ✓ perfect.
2. Truss with 7 joints needs **11** members.
3. A square with 4 members: 2(4)−3 = 5 > 4, so deficient: it can collapse into a rhombus; add one diagonal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting a member passing over another without a joint.
- Treating tension as negative inconsistently; choose: tension +, compression −.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1) Find support reactions using the whole truss. 2) Start at a joint with at most **two unknown** members. 3) Apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at the pin (a particle). 4) Move to the next joint. Assume all members in tension; a negative result means compression.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Equilateral truss ABC, AB = 4 m (A hinge, B roller), 10 kN down at C. By symmetry RA = RB = 5 kN.
Joint A: member AC makes 60° with AB. ΣFy: F_AC sin60° + 5 = 0 → **F_AC = −5.774 kN (compression)**. ΣFx: F_AB + F_AC cos60° = 0 → **F_AB = +2.887 kN (tension)**. By symmetry F_BC = −5.774 kN.

steps.title: Check at joint C
steps.body: Vertical: 2×5.774×sin60° = 10 ✓ (both compressive members push up on C against the 10 kN load).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Pass a section through ≤ 3 members whose forces are unknown; treat either side as a rigid body and use ΣM, ΣFx, ΣFy. Take moments about the **intersection point of two unknowns** to isolate the third.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Parallel-chord truss, span 12 m, depth 4 m, four 3 m panels, 10 kN at each of the three interior bottom joints (L1, L2, L3). RA = RB = 15 kN.
Cut the panel between L1 and L2. Moment about the top joint above L2 (x = 6 m): RA×6 − 10×3 = 60 kN·m = F_bottom × 4 → **F_bottom = 15 kN (tension)**; the top chord force = 60/4 = 15 kN compression (moment about L2).

steps.title: Zero-force members
steps.body:
- Two non-collinear members at an unloaded joint: both are zero.
- Three members at an unloaded joint, two collinear: the third is zero.
They still stabilise the truss and carry load under other loading.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Taking moments about a point not on two unknown lines of action.

lessons.title: Laws of dry friction and impending motion

scenes.text: A 50 kg fridge refuses to budge under a small push, then suddenly slides when you push harder.
Friction adjusts itself up to a limit, then drops a little once sliding starts.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
- Friction F opposes the (impending) relative motion and acts along the contact surface.
- **Static friction** adjusts: 0 ≤ F ≤ **Fmax = μs N**.
- **Kinetic friction** during sliding: **Fk = μk N**, with μk slightly less than μs.
- Independent of the apparent area of contact and (at moderate speeds) of the sliding speed.

**Angle of friction φ**: tan φ = μ = F/N. The total reaction R makes angle φ with the normal at limiting friction.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: 50 kg block on a floor, μs = 0.4, g = 9.81 m/s². N = 490.5 N, Fmax = 0.4×490.5 = **196.2 N**. A push of 150 N causes no motion; the friction force is then 150 N, not 196 N.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A horizontal push P on a 20 kg box with μ = 0.3 moves it at constant speed: P = μk W = 0.3×196.2 = **58.9 N**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing F = μN when the body is not on the verge of slipping.
- Using N = W on an incline or when other forces have vertical components.
- Believing a wider tyre gives more friction in the basic law.

scenes.text: A painter leans a uniform ladder on a smooth wall. The floor friction is μ = 0.4.

steps.title: Setup
steps.body: Smooth wall: reaction RW is horizontal. Floor: normal RF vertical and friction F = μRF horizontal (toward the wall). Equations: ΣFy: RF = W; ΣFx: F = RW; ΣM about the foot: RW L sinθ = W (L/2) cosθ.

steps.title: Derivation and answer
steps.body:
From moments: RW = (W/2) cotθ. At limiting friction F = μW = RW → μW = (W/2)cotθ → **tanθ = 1/(2μ)**.
μ = 0.4: tanθ = 1.25 → **θmin = 51.34°**.

steps.title: A person on the ladder
steps.body: If a person of weight P stands at fraction s of the length from the foot: RW = (W/2 + sP)cotθ, and the ladder is safe when RW ≤ μ(W+P). A person climbing higher makes the ladder more likely to slip.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using friction at the wall when the wall is declared smooth.
- Taking moments about the top; the foot eliminates both floor forces.
- Confusing angle with the wall and with the floor.

steps.title: Definitions & equations
steps.body:
Displacement s, velocity v = ds/dt, acceleration a = dv/dt = v dv/ds. For constant a:
- **v = u + at**
- **s = ut + ½at²**
- **v² = u² + 2as**
- s = (u+v)t/2
Convert units: 1 km/h = 1/3.6 m/s.

steps.title: Solved example 2 – braking
steps.body: u = 108 km/h = 30 m/s, a = −5 m/s². Stopping time t = 30/5 = **6 s**; distance = u²/2|a| = 900/10 = **90 m**.

steps.title: Calculus relations
steps.body: v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt; conversely **Δv = ∫a dt**, **Δs = ∫v dt**. Graphs: slope of s–t is v; slope of v–t is a; area under v–t is displacement; area under a–t is Δv. Total distance needs areas taken positively.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
s = t³ − 6t² + 9t → v = 3t² − 12t + 9 = 3(t−1)(t−3); a = 6t − 12.
v = 0 at **t = 1 s and t = 3 s**. s(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 = **4 m**; s(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 = **0 m**. At t = 1 s, a = −6 m/s²; at t = 3 s, a = +6 m/s².
Distance in 0–3 s: 4 m out + 4 m back = **8 m**, displacement 0.

steps.title: Graph reading
steps.body: A trapezoid v–t graph (accelerate, cruise, brake): total distance = area = ½(t_total + t_cruise)·v_max.

- Taking s(3) − s(0) as the distance when direction reverses.

steps.title: Statics

lessons.title: Environment, ecosystem and its components

scenes.text: A village pond holds algae, snails, fish, frogs, kingfishers, mud and sunlight.
Remove any one part and the rest change. That network of living and non-living parts is an ecosystem.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Environment** = the sum of physical, chemical and biological surroundings (air, water, land, living things) that affect an organism. **Ecology** studies relationships between organisms and environment. An **ecosystem** (Tansley, 1935) is a functional unit of living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) components interacting through energy flow and nutrient cycling. Levels: organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
- **Abiotic:** sunlight, temperature, water, soil, nutrients, gases.
- **Biotic:** **producers** (autotrophs: plants, algae), **consumers** (primary herbivores, secondary and tertiary carnivores, omnivores) and **decomposers** (bacteria, fungi) that recycle nutrients.
Functions: energy flow, nutrient cycling, productivity, decomposition, regulation.

steps.title: Worked classification
steps.body: In a pond: phytoplankton = producers; zooplankton, tadpoles = primary consumers; small fish = secondary; kingfisher = tertiary; bacteria in mud = decomposers. Dissolved O₂ and temperature are abiotic factors that limit fish.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling decomposers 'consumers'; they are a separate functional group.
- Thinking an ecosystem must be large: a rotting log is one.
- Mixing habitat (where an organism lives) with niche (its role).

lessons.title: Energy flow, food chains and ecological pyramids

scenes.text: Only about 1 percent of sunlight reaching a field is captured by plants.
By the time energy reaches a tiger, only a trickle remains. This is why top predators are rare.

steps.title: Energy flow
steps.body: Energy flows one way: sun → producers → consumers → decomposers, lost as heat at each step (second law of thermodynamics). **Lindeman's 10% law:** about **10%** of energy at one trophic level passes to the next. **Gross primary productivity (GPP)** − respiration (R) = **net primary productivity (NPP)**. Food chains: **grazing** (plant-based) and **detritus** (dead matter-based); interconnected chains form a **food web**.

steps.title: Ecological pyramids
steps.body: Pyramids of **number**, **biomass** and **energy**. Energy pyramids are *always upright*. Number pyramids can be inverted (one tree, many insects); biomass pyramids can be inverted in oceans (phytoplankton turn over quickly).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Producers fix 20 000 kJ/m²/yr. Herbivores ≈ 2000, secondary carnivores ≈ 200, tertiary ≈ **20 kJ/m²/yr**. GPP 8000, R 3000 → **NPP 5000**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 – biomagnification
steps.body: A persistent pesticide (e.g. DDT) at 0.01 ppm in water can reach ~25 ppm in fish-eating birds because it is fat-soluble and not excreted: concentration rises up the chain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy 'recycles' (matter does, energy does not).
- Believing 10 percent is exact; it varies from 5 to 20.

lessons.title: Biogeochemical cycles: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus

story.title: The atom that has been everywhere

scenes.text: A carbon atom in your breakfast may have been in a dinosaur, a tree and the sea.
Matter cycles between living things and the physical environment.

steps.title: Carbon cycle
steps.body: CO₂ in the air (~0.04% = ~420 ppm today) is fixed by **photosynthesis** into organic carbon, returned by **respiration, decomposition and combustion**. Large stores: oceans, fossil fuels, soils, limestone. Human burning of fossil fuels and deforestation add CO₂ faster than sinks remove it.

steps.title: Nitrogen cycle
steps.body: N₂ (78% of air) is unusable by most organisms. Steps: **nitrogen fixation** (Rhizobium in legume nodules, Azotobacter, lightning, Haber–Bosch) → **ammonification** (decomposers make NH₃/NH₄⁺) → **nitrification** (Nitrosomonas: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter: NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) → plant uptake (assimilation) → **denitrification** (Pseudomonas: NO₃⁻ → N₂). Excess fertiliser nitrate causes eutrophication.

steps.title: Phosphorus cycle
steps.body: A **sedimentary cycle** with no gaseous phase: weathering of rock releases phosphate; plants absorb it; animals eat plants; decomposers release it; runoff carries it to the sea where it sediments. Phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient in fresh water.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Why do farmers rotate pulses with cereals? Legume roots host Rhizobium that fix atmospheric N₂, enriching soil nitrate for the next crop and reducing the need for urea.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing nitrification (to nitrate) with denitrification (back to N₂).
- Treating phosphorus as gaseous.

activity.prompt: Order the nitrogen cycle steps starting from atmospheric N₂.
items: Nitrogen fixation: N₂ → ammonia/ammonium
Nitrification: ammonium → nitrite → nitrate

Denitrification: nitrate → N₂ returned to the air

quiz.why: Algal blooms deplete O₂.

lessons.title: Ecological succession and major ecosystems

story.title: A bare rock becomes a forest

scenes.text: After a lava flow, bare rock is first colonised by lichens, then mosses, grasses, shrubs and trees over centuries.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Succession
steps.body: **Ecological succession** is the orderly, directional change of communities over time until a stable **climax community**. **Primary succession** begins on lifeless surfaces (bare rock, new sand dune, lava); **secondary succession** on land that had soil (abandoned farmland, after fire/flood) and is faster. Sere stages: pioneer species → seral communities → climax. **Hydrosere** = on water (pond → marsh → meadow → forest); **lithosere** = on rock.

steps.title: Ecosystem types
steps.body:
- **Forest:** tropical rain forest (highest biodiversity), temperate deciduous, taiga.
- **Grassland:** savanna, prairie, steppe.
- **Desert:** < 25 cm rainfall, adapted xerophytes.
- **Aquatic:** freshwater (ponds, lakes, rivers), estuaries (very productive), marine, wetlands.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Lichens secrete acids that weather rock into soil – they are the pioneers of a lithosere, preparing conditions for mosses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling succession 'growth' of a single plant.
- Thinking the climax is the same everywhere; it depends on climate.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body: **Density** = total individuals / total area sampled. **Frequency (%)** = (quadrats in which the species occurs / total quadrats) × 100. **Abundance** = total individuals / quadrats in which it occurs.

steps.title: Observation table

10 quadrats of 1 m²; species A found in 6 quadrats; total 45 individuals.
- Density = 45/10 = **4.5 per m²**
- Frequency = 6/10 = **60 %**
- Abundance = 45/6 = **7.5 per occupied quadrat**

courses.title: Maths I · Unit 1 · Differential calculus of one variable
courses.summary: Successive differentiation, Leibniz theorem, mean value theorems, Taylor–Maclaurin expansions and indeterminate forms, covering topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech/B.E. first-year programmes.
outcomes: Find nth derivatives using standard results and Leibniz theorem
State and apply Rolle's, Lagrange's and Cauchy's mean value theorems
Expand functions in Taylor and Maclaurin series
Evaluate indeterminate forms with L'Hôpital's rule
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Riya models beam deflection as y = x²·e^(3x) and needs the 5th derivative for a series solution.
Differentiating five times by hand is messy — Leibniz theorem does it in one line.

steps.title: Standard nth derivatives
steps.body:
- dⁿ/dxⁿ (e^(ax)) = aⁿ e^(ax)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ (ax+b)^m = m(m−1)…(m−n+1) aⁿ (ax+b)^(m−n)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ 1/(ax+b) = (−1)ⁿ n! aⁿ /(ax+b)^(n+1)
- dⁿ/dxⁿ log(ax+b) = (−1)^(n−1) (n−1)! aⁿ /(ax+b)ⁿ
- dⁿ/dxⁿ sin(ax+b) = aⁿ sin(ax+b+nπ/2); same with cos.

For rational functions, first split into **partial fractions**, then apply the 1/(ax+b) rule to each term.

steps.title: Leibniz theorem
steps.body:
If u and v have nth derivatives, (uv)ₙ = Σ (r=0 to n) ⁿCᵣ u₍ₙ₋ᵣ₎ vᵣ = uₙv + ⁿC₁u₍ₙ₋₁₎v₁ + ⁿC₂u₍ₙ₋₂₎v₂ + … + uvₙ.

Choose **v** to be the polynomial factor, because its derivatives vanish after a few steps.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Find y₅ for y = x²e^(3x).
Take u = e^(3x), v = x². v₁ = 2x, v₂ = 2, v₃ = 0.
y₅ = 3⁵e^(3x)x² + 5·3⁴e^(3x)·2x + 10·3³e^(3x)·2 = e^(3x)(243x² + 810x + 540).

**Example 2.** Find yₙ for y = 1/(x²−1).
Partial fractions: y = ½[1/(x−1) − 1/(x+1)].
yₙ = ½(−1)ⁿ n! [1/(x−1)^(n+1) − 1/(x+1)^(n+1)].

steps.title: Classic exam result
steps.body:
**Example 3.** If y = sin⁻¹x, show (1−x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0 and hence (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ − (2n+1)x y₍ₙ₊₁₎ − n²yₙ = 0.
Step 1: y₁ = 1/√(1−x²) ⇒ (1−x²)y₁² = 1.
Step 2: differentiate: (1−x²)2y₁y₂ − 2xy₁² = 0 ⇒ (1−x²)y₂ − xy₁ = 0.
Step 3: apply Leibniz n times to each product: (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ + n(−2x)y₍ₙ₊₁₎ + [n(n−1)/2](−2)yₙ − [x y₍ₙ₊₁₎ + n yₙ] = 0, which simplifies to the result.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the factor aⁿ from the chain rule.
- Using Leibniz with the exponential as v — the series never terminates.
- Missing the binomial coefficient ⁿC₂ = n(n−1)/2 when collecting terms.

activity.prompt: Match each function with its nth derivative

quiz.why: Each differentiation multiplies e^(−x) by −1, so the third derivative is (−1)³e^(−x) = −e^(−x).

quiz.q: In Leibniz theorem for (uv)ₙ the coefficient of u₍ₙ₋₂₎v₂ is
quiz.why: In (uv)ₙ, the term with u_{n−2}v₂ has coefficient ⁿC₂ = n(n − 1)/2.

quiz.q: For y = x³ sin x, which factor should be v in Leibniz?
quiz.why: Take v = x³, since its derivatives vanish after the third, leaving only four terms in Leibniz's formula.
d/dx cos 3x = 3cos(3x + π/2), so each derivative gives a factor 3 and a phase shift π/2: 3ⁿcos(3x + nπ/2).
For log(ax + b), the nth derivative is (−1)^(n−1)(n − 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ. With a = 2 this gives the stated result.

scenes.text: A car covers 120 km in 1.5 h on an expressway with an 80 km/h limit.
Without any camera seeing it speed, the mean value theorem proves that at some instant the speed was exactly 80 km/h.

steps.title: Rolle's theorem
steps.body:
If f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) and f(a) = f(b), then there is at least one c in (a,b) with f′(c) = 0.

Geometrically: a smooth curve that starts and ends at the same height has a horizontal tangent somewhere in between.

steps.title: Lagrange (LMVT) and Cauchy MVT
steps.body:
**LMVT:** f continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b) ⇒ ∃ c ∈ (a,b): f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a). The tangent at c is parallel to the chord.

**Cauchy MVT:** f, g continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), g′(x) ≠ 0 ⇒ ∃ c: f′(c)/g′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/[g(b) − g(a)].

LMVT is Cauchy's with g(x) = x; Rolle's is LMVT with f(a) = f(b).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x² − 5x + 6 on [2,3].
f(2) = 0 = f(3); polynomial ⇒ continuous and differentiable. f′(c) = 2c − 5 = 0 ⇒ c = 2.5 ∈ (2,3). ✔

**Example 2.** Find c for LMVT with f(x) = x³ on [1,3].
[f(3) − f(1)]/(3 − 1) = (27 − 1)/2 = 13. f′(c) = 3c² = 13 ⇒ c = √(13/3) ≈ 2.08 ∈ (1,3). ✔

**Example 3.** Using LMVT show sin x < x for x > 0 (x ≤ π/2 suffices).
f(t) = t − sin t on [0,x]: f(x) − f(0) = x·f′(c) = x(1 − cos c) > 0 ⇒ x > sin x.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Rolle's to f(x) = |x| on [−1,1]: it is not differentiable at 0, so the theorem does not apply.
- Reporting a c that lies outside the open interval.
- In Cauchy MVT, forgetting to check g′(x) ≠ 0 in (a,b).

activity.prompt: LMVT for f(x) = x² on [1, 5]: find c.

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem needs f(a) = f(b) and
quiz.why: Rolle's theorem needs f continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b). Then f′(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
options: only differentiability at a and b

quiz.why: The Lagrange MVT says there is a point where the tangent is parallel to the chord joining the end points, because f′(c) equals the chord's slope.
options: a tangent parallel to the chord exists
the curve is a straight line

quiz.q: Rolle's theorem fails for |x| on [−1,1] because
quiz.why: |x| has a corner at 0, so it is not differentiable there, and Rolle's theorem needs differentiability on the open interval. (f(−1) = f(1) and it is continuous.)
options: it is not differentiable at x = 0

quiz.q: c for LMVT with f(x) = eˣ on [0,1]?
quiz.why: f′(c) = (e − 1)/(1 − 0) gives eᶜ = e − 1, so c = ln(e − 1) ≈ 0.541, which lies in (0, 1).

quiz.q: Cauchy MVT with g(x) = x reduces to
quiz.why: With g(x) = x, g′ = 1 and g(b) − g(a) = b − a, so Cauchy's formula becomes Lagrange's: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a).

scenes.text: A microcontroller has no 'sin' button — it only adds and multiplies.
Engineers store a few Maclaurin terms of sin x and get 6-digit accuracy for small angles.

steps.title: Taylor's theorem
steps.body:
f(a + h) = f(a) + h f′(a) + h²/2! f″(a) + … + hⁿ⁻¹/(n−1)! f⁽ⁿ⁻¹⁾(a) + Rₙ.

Lagrange remainder: Rₙ = hⁿ/n! f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh), 0 < θ < 1. Writing x = a + h gives the series in powers of (x − a). With a = 0 we get the **Maclaurin** series.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Expand log x in powers of (x − 1) up to 4 terms.
f(1) = 0, f′ = 1/x → 1, f″ = −1/x² → −1, f‴ = 2/x³ → 2, f⁗ = −6/x⁴ → −6.
log x = (x−1) − (x−1)²/2 + (x−1)³/3 − (x−1)⁴/4 + …

**Example 2.** Maclaurin series of eˣ sin x up to x³.
Multiply series: (1 + x + x²/2 + x³/6)(x − x³/6) = x + x² + (1/2 − 1/6)x³ + … = x + x² + x³/3 + …

**Example 3.** Estimate √(1.1) using (1+x)^(1/2): 1 + 0.05 − 0.00125 + 0.0000625 ≈ 1.04881 (true value 1.048809).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing hⁿ/n instead of hⁿ/n! in the coefficients.
- Using log(1 + x) outside −1 < x ≤ 1.
- Expanding about 0 when the question asks for powers of (x − a).

activity.prompt: Complete the Maclaurin series
activity.text: cos x = 1 − x²/___ + x⁴/24 − …   and   eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/___ + …

quiz.q: Coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin series of sin x?
quiz.why: sin x = x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …, so the coefficient of x³ is −1/6.

quiz.q: Maclaurin series is Taylor series about
quiz.why: The Maclaurin series is the Taylor series expanded about the point x = 0.

quiz.q: tan x up to x³ is
quiz.why: tan x = x + x³/3 + 2x⁵/15 + …, so up to x³ it is x + x³/3.
The Lagrange form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem is Rₙ = (hⁿ/n!) f⁽ⁿ⁾(a + θh) with 0 < θ < 1.

quiz.q: First two non-zero terms of e^x·cos x?
quiz.why: Multiplying (1 + x + x²/2 + …)(1 − x²/2 + …) gives 1 + x + 0·x² − x³/3 + …, so the first two non-zero terms are 1 + x.

scenes.text: Arjun is told sin x / x → 1 as x → 0 but wonders why we cannot just put x = 0.
0/0 is not a number — it is an indeterminate form that needs a rule.

steps.title: Forms and the rule
steps.body:
Indeterminate forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞ − ∞, 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰.

**L'Hôpital:** if f(x)/g(x) → 0/0 or ∞/∞ as x → a, then lim f/g = lim f′/g′, provided the latter exists. Differentiate numerator and denominator **separately** (not the quotient rule).

steps.title: Converting other forms
steps.body:
- 0·∞: write f·g = f/(1/g).
- ∞ − ∞: combine into a single fraction.
- 0⁰, 1^∞, ∞⁰: let y = f^g, take log y = g·log f, find its limit L, then answer = e^L.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** lim (x→0) (1 − cos x)/x² = lim sin x/(2x) = lim cos x/2 = 1/2.

**Example 2.** lim (x→0) (1 + x)^(1/x) — form 1^∞. log y = log(1 + x)/x → (1/(1 + x))/1 → 1 ⇒ limit = e.

**Example 3.** lim (x→0⁺) x log x — form 0·(−∞). Write log x/(1/x) → (1/x)/(−1/x²) = −x → 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the rule when the form is not 0/0 or ∞/∞ (e.g. lim (x→0) (x+1)/x).
- Using the quotient rule on f/g.
- Forgetting to exponentiate back after taking logs.

activity.prompt: Sort each limit by its indeterminate form

quiz.why: (eˣ − 1)/x is of the form 0/0. L'Hôpital gives eˣ/1 → 1.
Let y = (cos x)^(1/x²). ln y = ln cos x/x² → (−tan x)/(2x) → −1/2 by L'Hôpital, so y → e^(−1/2).
L'Hôpital's rule says the limit of f/g equals the limit of f′/g′, that is, the numerator and denominator are differentiated separately, not by the quotient rule.
options: the whole fraction by quotient rule

quiz.q: Which is NOT an indeterminate form?
quiz.why: 0/∞ is not indeterminate; it tends to 0. The others (∞ − ∞, 1^∞, 0/0) are indeterminate forms.
(x − sin x)/x³ → (1 − cos x)/(3x²) → sin x/(6x) → 1/6 by repeated L'Hôpital (or from the series x³/6).

questions.q: nth derivative of e^(5x)
questions.why: d/dx e^(5x) = 5e^(5x), so the nth derivative is 5ⁿe^(5x).

questions.q: Maclaurin series is a Taylor expansion about
questions.why: A Maclaurin series is a Taylor series about a = 0.

questions.q: Which function satisfies Rolle's theorem on [0, π]?
questions.why: sin x is continuous and differentiable on [0, π] with sin 0 = sin π = 0, so Rolle's theorem applies. tan x and 1/x are not continuous on [0, π], and |x − 1| is not differentiable at 1.

questions.q: lim (x→0) sin 3x / x =
questions.why: By L'Hôpital, sin 3x/x → 3cos 3x/1 = 3 as x → 0.

questions.q: In (uv)ₙ, number of terms in Leibniz expansion is
questions.why: Leibniz's expansion (uv)ₙ = Σ ⁿC_r u_{n−r}v_r runs from r = 0 to n, which gives n + 1 terms.

questions.q: Assertion (A): For f(x) = x^(2/3) on [−1,1], Rolle's theorem cannot be applied.  Reason (R): f is not differentiable at x = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: f(−1) = f(1) = 1, but f′(x) = (2/3)x^(−1/3) does not exist at 0, so differentiability on (−1, 1) fails. This explains why Rolle's theorem cannot be applied.

questions.q: c of LMVT for f(x) = log x on [1, e]
questions.why: LMVT: f′(c) = 1/c = (ln e − ln 1)/(e − 1) = 1/(e − 1), so c = e − 1 ≈ 1.718, which is in (1, e).

questions.q: Coefficient of x² in Maclaurin series of log(1 + x)
questions.why: ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …, so the coefficient of x² is −1/2.
Let y = (1 + 2/x)ˣ. ln y = x ln(1 + 2/x) → 2, so y → e².

questions.q: If y = e^(ax)·x, then y₃ =
questions.why: By Leibniz with u = e^(ax) and v = x: y₃ = x·a³e^(ax) + 3·1·a²e^(ax) = a²e^(ax)(ax + 3).

questions.q: Case: A sensor's output is f(t) = t³ − 3t on [0, √3]. A student claims the rate is zero somewhere inside. Using Rolle's theorem, the instant is
questions.why: f(0) = 0 and f(√3) = 3√3 − 3√3 = 0, so Rolle applies. f′(t) = 3t² − 3 = 0 gives t = 1, which lies in (0, √3).

questions.why: 1/x − 1/sin x = (sin x − x)/(x sin x) ≈ (−x³/6)/x² = −x/6 → 0.

questions.q: If y = sin⁻¹x, value of y₅ at x = 0 (using (1−x²)y₍ₙ₊₂₎ − (2n+1)xy₍ₙ₊₁₎ − n²yₙ = 0)
questions.why: At x = 0 the recurrence reduces to y_{n+2} = n²yₙ. With y₁ = 1: y₃ = 1² × 1 = 1 and y₅ = 3² × y₃ = 9.

lim (x→0) (a^x − b^x)/x
questions.why: By L'Hôpital, (aˣ − bˣ)/x → aˣ ln a − bˣ ln b → ln a − ln b = ln(a/b).

courses.summary: Partial derivatives, total derivative and chain rule, Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, Jacobians, errors, maxima–minima of two variables and Lagrange multipliers.
outcomes: Compute partial and total derivatives using the chain rule
Apply Euler's theorem and its corollaries

Find extrema with and without constraints

lessons.title: Partial derivatives, total derivative and chain rule

scenes.text: Temperature on a plate is T(x,y) = 100 − x² − 2y².
An ant walks along a path x(t), y(t). How fast does the temperature it feels change? Chain rule.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: For u = f(x,y): ∂u/∂x is the derivative with y held constant; ∂u/∂y with x held constant. Higher orders: ∂²u/∂x², ∂²u/∂x∂y. For smooth functions the mixed partials are equal (∂²u/∂x∂y = ∂²u/∂y∂x).

steps.title: Total derivative and chain rule
steps.body:
If u = f(x,y), x = x(t), y = y(t): du/dt = ∂u/∂x · dx/dt + ∂u/∂y · dy/dt.
If x = x(r,s), y = y(r,s): ∂u/∂r = uₓ xᵣ + u_y yᵣ.
Implicit function f(x,y) = 0: dy/dx = −fₓ/f_y.
Total differential: du = uₓ dx + u_y dy (used for small errors).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x²y + y³, x = t², y = 2t. du/dt = (2xy)(2t) + (x² + 3y²)(2). Here 2xy = 4t³, ×2t = 8t⁴; x² + 3y² = t⁴ + 12t², ×2 = 2t⁴ + 24t². du/dt = 10t⁴ + 24t². (Check by substitution: u = 2t⁵ + 8t³ ⇒ 10t⁴ + 24t² ✔)

**Example 2.** x³ + y³ = 3axy. dy/dx = −(3x² − 3ay)/(3y² − 3ax) = (ay − x²)/(y² − ax).

**Example 3 (errors).** Area of a rectangle A = xy, x = 10 m, y = 5 m, each measured with error 0.01 m. dA = y dx + x dy = 5(0.01) + 10(0.01) = 0.15 m² (percentage 0.3%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the other variable as a function while doing ∂/∂x.
- Dropping the minus sign in dy/dx = −fₓ/f_y.
- Adding absolute errors without converting to percentage when asked for % error.

activity.prompt: u = x²y, x = 2, y = 3. If x increases by 0.01 and y by 0.02, approximate change du (= 2xy dx + x² dy).

quiz.why: Treat y as a constant: ∂/∂x(x²y³) = 2xy³.
For an implicit function f(x, y) = 0, dy/dx = −f_x/f_y.
For a function with continuous second partial derivatives, mixed partials are equal (Clairaut/Schwarz theorem).
For u = e^(xy), differentiating with respect to y treats x as constant: ∂u/∂y = x e^(xy).

quiz.q: Percentage error in A = πr² if r has 1% error
quiz.why: dA/A = 2dr/r, so a 1% error in r gives a 2% error in A = πr².

scenes.text: An economist's output Q = K^0.3 L^0.7 doubles when both inputs double.
That is homogeneity of degree 1 — Euler's theorem gives x Qₓ + y Q_y = Q.

steps.title: Homogeneous functions
steps.body:
u(x,y) is homogeneous of degree n if u(tx, ty) = tⁿ u(x,y), equivalently u = xⁿ φ(y/x).

**Euler:** x ∂u/∂x + y ∂u/∂y = n u.
**Corollary:** x²uₓₓ + 2xy uₓᵧ + y²u_yy = n(n − 1)u.

steps.title: When u itself is not homogeneous
steps.body:
If f(u) is homogeneous of degree n, then x uₓ + y u_y = n f(u)/f′(u) = g(u).
Second order: x²uₓₓ + 2xy uₓᵧ + y²u_yy = g(u)[g′(u) − 1].

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x³ + y³ + 3x²y: degree 3 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y = 3u. (Check: x(3x² + 6xy) + y(3y² + 3x²) = 3x³ + 9x²y + 3y³ = 3u ✔)

**Example 2.** u = sin⁻¹[(x² + y²)/(x + y)]. sin u is homogeneous of degree 1 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y = sin u/cos u = tan u.

**Example 3.** For Example 2, second order: g = tan u, g′ = sec²u ⇒ x²uₓₓ + 2xyuₓᵧ + y²u_yy = tan u (sec²u − 1) = tan³u.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a function homogeneous when terms have different degrees (x² + y).
- Forgetting n(n − 1) in the second-order corollary.
- Applying Euler to u directly when only sin u or tan u is homogeneous.

activity.prompt: Degree of homogeneity

quiz.why: u = x⁴ + y⁴ is homogeneous of degree 4, so Euler's theorem gives x u_x + y u_y = 4u.
tan⁻¹(y/x) is homogeneous of degree 0, so by Euler x u_x + y u_y = 0·u = 0.

quiz.q: If u is homogeneous of degree 3, x²uₓₓ + 2xyuₓᵧ + y²u_yy =
quiz.why: For a homogeneous function of degree n, x²u_xx + 2xy u_xy + y²u_yy = n(n − 1)u. With n = 3 this is 6u.

quiz.q: u = log[(x² + y²)/(x + y)]: e^u homogeneous of degree 1 ⇒ xuₓ + yu_y =
quiz.why: e^u = (x² + y²)/(x + y) is homogeneous of degree 1. For f = e^u, x u_x + y u_y = n f/f′ = e^u/e^u = 1.
A homogeneous function has all terms of the same degree. x² has degree 2 but 3y has degree 1, so it is not homogeneous.

scenes.text: Kabir integrates over a circular disc and switches to polar coordinates.
The factor r in dx dy = r dr dθ is a Jacobian.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body:
J = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) = det[[uₓ, u_y],[vₓ, v_y]].
- Chain: ∂(u,v)/∂(r,s) = ∂(u,v)/∂(x,y) · ∂(x,y)/∂(r,s)
- Inverse: J · J′ = 1 where J′ = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v)
- **Functional dependence:** u, v are functionally related (dependent) iff J = 0 identically.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. ∂(x,y)/∂(r,θ) = cos θ·r cos θ − (−r sin θ)·sin θ = r.

**Example 2.** Spherical: x = r sinθ cosφ, y = r sinθ sinφ, z = r cosθ ⇒ ∂(x,y,z)/∂(r,θ,φ) = r² sin θ.

**Example 3.** u = x + y, v = xy. J = det[[1,1],[y,x]] = x − y; so ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) = 1/(x − y).

steps.title: Testing dependence
steps.body: **Example 4.** u = (x + y)/(1 − xy), v = tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y. Compute J: uₓ = (1 + y²)/(1 − xy)², u_y = (1 + x²)/(1 − xy)², vₓ = 1/(1 + x²), v_y = 1/(1 + y²). J = [(1+y²)/(1+y²) − (1+x²)/(1+x²)]/(1 − xy)² = 0 ⇒ dependent. Indeed u = tan v.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping rows/columns inconsistently (changes the sign).
- Forgetting |J| (absolute value) when changing variables in integrals.
- Concluding dependence from J = 0 at a single point — it must vanish identically.

activity.prompt: Match the transformation with its Jacobian
pairs: u = x + y, v = x − y

quiz.why: For x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ the Jacobian ∂(x, y)/∂(r, θ) = r.
The Jacobians of inverse transformations are reciprocals: J·J′ = 1, so J′ = 1/4.

quiz.q: u, v are functionally dependent iff J is
quiz.why: Two functions are functionally dependent exactly when their Jacobian vanishes identically.
For spherical coordinates the Jacobian ∂(x, y, z)/∂(r, θ, φ) = r² sin θ.

lessons.title: Maxima and minima of functions of two variables

scenes.text: A packaging engineer wants the open box of volume 32 cm³ with the least cardboard.
That is minimising S(x,y) — critical points plus the second-derivative test.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Solve fₓ = 0, f_y = 0 for critical points.
2. At each, r = fₓₓ, s = fₓᵧ, t = f_yy.
3. rt − s² > 0 and r < 0 ⇒ **maximum**; rt − s² > 0 and r > 0 ⇒ **minimum**; rt − s² < 0 ⇒ **saddle point**; rt − s² = 0 ⇒ further investigation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** f = x³ + y³ − 3axy (a > 0). fₓ = 3x² − 3ay = 0, f_y = 3y² − 3ax = 0 ⇒ (0,0), (a,a).
r = 6x, s = −3a, t = 6y.
At (0,0): rt − s² = −9a² < 0 ⇒ saddle.
At (a,a): 36a² − 9a² > 0, r = 6a > 0 ⇒ minimum, f = −a³.

**Example 2.** Open box volume 32: S = xy + 64/x + 64/y (with z = 32/(xy), S = xy + 2xz + 2yz). Sₓ = y − 64/x² = 0, S_y = x − 64/y² = 0 ⇒ x = y = 4, z = 2. r = 128/x³ = 2 > 0, rt − s² = 4 − 1 = 3 > 0 ⇒ minimum, S = 48 cm².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding max/min from fₓ = f_y = 0 alone.
- Using rt − s² with s = fₓ instead of fₓᵧ.
- Ignoring points where the test is inconclusive.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to classify a critical point
items: Compute fₓ and f_y
Solve fₓ = 0 and f_y = 0
Find r = fₓₓ, s = fₓᵧ, t = f_yy at the point
Evaluate rt − s²
Use the sign of rt − s² and r to decide

quiz.q: rt − s² > 0, r < 0 at a critical point ⇒
quiz.why: At a critical point, if rt − s² > 0 and r < 0, the function has a local maximum.
If rt − s² < 0 at a critical point, it is a saddle point (neither max nor min).

quiz.q: Critical point of f = x² + y² − 4x + 6y
quiz.why: f_x = 2x − 4 = 0 and f_y = 2y + 6 = 0 give x = 2 and y = −3.

quiz.q: For f = x² − y², origin is
quiz.why: For f = x² − y², r = 2, t = −2, s = 0, so rt − s² = −4 < 0, a saddle at the origin.
At (2, −3), f = 4 + 9 − 8 − 18 = −13, a minimum since rt − s² = 4 > 0 and r > 0.

scenes.text: A satellite dish feed must lie on the paraboloid while minimising distance to a point.
When a constraint links the variables, Lagrange multipliers turn it into an unconstrained system.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Extremise f(x,y,z) subject to φ(x,y,z) = 0.
Form F = f + λφ. Solve Fₓ = 0, F_y = 0, F_z = 0 together with φ = 0. The solutions are the stationary points; the nature is usually decided from the physical problem.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Maximise xyz subject to x + y + z = 12.
F = xyz + λ(x + y + z − 12): yz + λ = 0, xz + λ = 0, xy + λ = 0 ⇒ yz = xz = xy ⇒ x = y = z = 4, max = 64.

**Example 2.** Minimise x² + y² + z² subject to x + y + z = 3a.
2x + λ = 0 etc. ⇒ x = y = z = a, min = 3a².

**Example 3.** Rectangular box of volume V with least surface: by symmetry and Lagrange, x = y = z = V^(1/3) (a cube).

steps.title: Shortcut checks
steps.body: Symmetric functions with symmetric constraints usually have the extremum at equal variables — use this to check your answer, not to replace the working in an exam.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to use the constraint equation itself.
- Dividing by a variable that could be zero (check those cases separately).
- Reporting λ as the answer — λ is only a helper.

questions.why: A critical point is a saddle point when rt − s² < 0.

questions.why: u = (x² + y²)/(x + y) is homogeneous of degree 1, so x u_x + y u_y = u.

questions.why: f_x = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1 and f_y = 2y = 0 gives y = 0. The stationary points are (1, 0) and (−1, 0).

questions.why: At (1, 0): r = 6x = 6, t = 2, s = 0. Then rt − s² = 12 > 0 and r > 0, so it is a minimum.

questions.q: Assertion (A): u = sin⁻¹(x/y) satisfies xuₓ + yu_y = 0.  Reason (R): u is a homogeneous function of degree 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A

questions.q: If x = u(1 − v), y = uv, then ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) =
questions.why: The Jacobian is the determinant of [[1 − v, −u], [v, u]] = u(1 − v) + uv = u.

questions.q: u = sin⁻¹[(x + y)/(√x + √y)]: xuₓ + yu_y =
questions.why: sin u = (x + y)/(√x + √y) is homogeneous of degree 1/2. Then x u_x + y u_y = (1/2) sin u/cos u = (1/2) tan u.

questions.q: Case: Temperature T = 400xyz² on the sphere x² + y² + z² = 1. Using Lagrange, the highest temperature is
questions.why: By Lagrange multipliers x² = y² = 1/4 and z² = 1/2 give the extremum: T = 400 × (1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 50.

questions.why: The distance from the origin to the plane is 9/√(1 + 4 + 4) = 9/3 = 3, so the minimum of distance squared is 9.

questions.q: If u = f(y − z, z − x, x − y), then uₓ + u_y + u_z =
questions.why: For u = f(y − z, z − x, x − y), the partial derivatives contributed by the arguments cancel in pairs in u_x + u_y + u_z, so the sum is 0.

questions.q: x = e^u cos v, y = e^u sin v: ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v) =
questions.why: The Jacobian = x_u y_v − x_v y_u = e^u cos v × e^u cos v + e^u sin v × e^u sin v = e^(2u)(cos²v + sin²v) = e^(2u).

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Γ(n) = ∫₀^∞ e^(−x) x^(n−1) dx (n > 0). Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n); Γ(n + 1) = n! for integer n; Γ(1/2) = √π.
B(m,n) = ∫₀¹ x^(m−1)(1 − x)^(n−1) dx = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Γ(n) = n! (it is (n − 1)!).
- Forgetting the factor ½ in the trig formula.
- Wrong substitution limits when converting to a Gamma integral.

quiz.why: Γ(1/2) = √π, a standard value of the gamma function.

lessons.title: Double integrals and change of order

scenes.text: A floor slab carries load intensity w(x,y). Total load = ∬ w dA.
Sometimes integrating in the other order turns a hard integral into an easy one.

steps.title: Evaluating ∬
steps.body:
∬_R f dx dy over R: integrate the inner variable between its curve limits, then the outer between constants.

**Change of order:** sketch the region, then re-describe it with horizontal strips instead of vertical ones (or vice versa) and write new limits.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∫₀¹∫₀^x (x² + y²) dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x³ + x³/3) dx = ∫₀¹ (4/3)x³ dx = 1/3.

**Example 2.** Change order and evaluate ∫₀^∞∫ₓ^∞ (e^(−y)/y) dy dx.
Region: 0 ≤ x ≤ y < ∞. New order: y from 0 to ∞, x from 0 to y.
∫₀^∞ (e^(−y)/y)·y dy = ∫₀^∞ e^(−y) dy = 1.

**Example 3.** Area between y = x² and y = x: ∫₀¹∫_(x²)^x dy dx = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/6.

steps.title: Sketch first
steps.body: Mark intersection points of the boundary curves. A vertical strip (dy inner) has y from lower curve to upper curve; a horizontal strip (dx inner) has x from left curve to right curve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving variable limits on the outer integral.
- Changing the order of the limits without redrawing the region.
- Integrating with respect to the wrong variable first.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫₀² ∫₀³ xy dy dx

quiz.q: Area enclosed by y = x and y = x² is
quiz.why: The curves meet at x = 0 and x = 1, so area = ∫₀¹(x − x²)dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6.

quiz.q: After changing order of ∫₀¹∫ₓ¹ f dy dx, the limits become
quiz.why: The region is 0 ≤ x ≤ y ≤ 1. Reversing the order gives y from 0 to 1 and x from 0 to y: ∫₀¹∫₀^y f dx dy.
The outer integral's limits must be constants, so that the result is a number and not a function.

scenes.text: The base of a tank is a disc of radius a. Integrating e^(−(x²+y²)) over it in x, y is painful.
In polar form, dx dy = r dr dθ and the integral becomes simple.

steps.title: Transformation
steps.body: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, dx dy = r dr dθ. In general ∬ f(x,y) dx dy = ∬ f(x(u,v), y(u,v)) |J| du dv with J = ∂(x,y)/∂(u,v).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∬ over x² + y² ≤ a² of (x² + y²) dx dy = ∫₀^(2π)∫₀^a r²·r dr dθ = 2π a⁴/4 = πa⁴/2.

**Example 2 (Gaussian).** I = ∫₀^∞ e^(−x²) dx. I² = ∫₀^(π/2)∫₀^∞ e^(−r²) r dr dθ = (π/2)(1/2) ⇒ I = √π/2.

**Example 3.** Area of the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ): ∫₀^(2π) ½a²(1 + cos θ)² dθ = ½a²(2π + π) = 3πa²/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

scenes.text: Vikram has 4 sensor equations but suspects only 3 carry new information.
The rank of the coefficient matrix tells him exactly how many are independent.

steps.title: Definition and methods
steps.body:
Rank ρ(A) = order of the largest non-vanishing minor = number of non-zero rows in row-echelon form = number of linearly independent rows (or columns).

Elementary row operations (swap, scale by non-zero, add a multiple of another row) do not change rank.

steps.title: Useful facts
steps.body:
- ρ(A) ≤ min(m, n) for m × n A.
- ρ(A) = n for an n × n matrix iff det A ≠ 0 (non-singular).
- ρ(AB) ≤ min(ρ(A), ρ(B)).
- Normal form [[Iᵣ, 0],[0, 0]] has rank r.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using column operations while solving equations (fine for rank only).
- Stopping before the matrix is fully in echelon form.
- Arithmetic slips — always check with a determinant when the matrix is square.

quiz.why: The 3 × 3 identity matrix is non-singular, with 3 independent rows, so its rank is 3.

quiz.q: Rank of a non-zero 3×4 matrix is at most
quiz.why: Rank cannot exceed the smaller of the number of rows and columns, so a 3 × 4 matrix has rank at most 3.
Elementary row operations do not change the rank of a matrix.

quiz.q: If det A = 0 for 3×3 A, rank is
quiz.why: If det A = 0 the matrix is singular and cannot have full rank, so its rank is less than 3.
The second row is half the first, so there is only one independent row and the rank is 1.

scenes.text: Flow balance at four junctions gives four equations in four unknown flows.
Is there a unique answer, many, or none? Compare ρ(A) and ρ([A|B]).

steps.title: Consistency (Rouché–Capelli)
steps.body:
For AX = B with n unknowns:
- ρ(A) ≠ ρ([A|B]) ⇒ inconsistent (no solution)
- ρ(A) = ρ([A|B]) = n ⇒ unique solution
- ρ(A) = ρ([A|B]) = r < n ⇒ infinitely many solutions with n − r free parameters.
Homogeneous AX = 0 is always consistent; non-trivial solutions exist iff ρ(A) < n (det A = 0 for square A).

steps.body:
**Example 1.** x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1.
[A|B] → R₂ − R₁: [0,−2,0 | −4] ⇒ y = 2; R₃ − 2R₁: [0,−1,−3 | −11] ⇒ −2 − 3z = −11 ⇒ z = 3; x = 1. Unique: (1, 2, 3).

**Example 2.** For what λ, μ does x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + λz = μ have (i) no, (ii) unique, (iii) infinite solutions?
Reduce: R₂ − R₁ = [0,1,2|4], R₃ − R₂ = [0,0,λ−3 | μ−10].

steps.title: Gauss elimination vs Gauss–Jordan
steps.body: Gauss elimination stops at upper-triangular form and back-substitutes; Gauss–Jordan continues to reduced form so the answer reads off directly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing ρ(A) with n only, ignoring the augmented matrix.
- Forgetting that a homogeneous system always has the trivial solution.
- Sign errors during back-substitution.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
AX = λX, X ≠ 0. Characteristic equation |A − λI| = 0. For 3×3: λ³ − (tr A)λ² + (sum of principal 2×2 minors)λ − det A = 0.
Eigenvectors: solve (A − λI)X = 0 for each λ.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Σλᵢ = trace A, Πλᵢ = det A.
- Eigenvalues of A⁻¹ are 1/λ; of Aᵏ are λᵏ; of kA are kλ.
- Triangular matrix: eigenvalues are diagonal entries.
- Real symmetric matrix: real eigenvalues, orthogonal eigenvectors for distinct λ.
- A and Aᵀ have the same eigenvalues.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the eigenvector as the zero vector.
- Sign error in the λ² coefficient of the 3×3 characteristic polynomial.
- Assuming every matrix has n independent eigenvectors.

quiz.why: If AX = λX then A⁻¹X = (1/λ)X, so 1/λ is an eigenvalue of A⁻¹.

steps.title: Cayley–Hamilton
steps.body:
Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. If |A − λI| = λ² − 5λ + 6, then A² − 5A + 6I = 0.
Uses: A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/6 from multiplying by A⁻¹; higher powers reduce to combinations of I and A.

steps.title: Diagonalisation and quadratic forms
steps.body:
If A has n independent eigenvectors, P = [X₁ … Xₙ] gives P⁻¹AP = D = diag(λᵢ) and Aᵏ = P Dᵏ P⁻¹. For symmetric A use orthonormal eigenvectors: Pᵀ A P = D (orthogonal reduction).
Quadratic form Q = XᵀAX: positive definite if all λ > 0; negative definite if all λ < 0; indefinite if mixed signs. Rank = number of non-zero λ, index = number of positive λ, signature = (positive − negative).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing the constant term as a number instead of a multiple of I.
- Putting eigenvectors in P in a different order from the λ in D.

courses.summary: Convergence of sequences and series, comparison, ratio, root and integral tests, alternating series and absolute convergence, and power series with radius of convergence.
outcomes: Decide convergence of sequences and standard series
Choose and apply comparison, ratio, root and integral tests

lessons.title: Sequences and the basics of series

scenes.text: Walk half the distance to a wall, then half the rest, and so on.
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … — infinitely many steps, yet a finite total of 1.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
A sequence aₙ converges to L if aₙ → L as n → ∞. A series Σaₙ converges if its partial sums Sₙ = a₁ + … + aₙ converge.

**nth-term test:** if Σaₙ converges then aₙ → 0. So if aₙ ↛ 0, the series diverges. (aₙ → 0 alone does NOT guarantee convergence.)

steps.title: Two benchmark series
steps.body:
- Geometric Σ rⁿ converges iff |r| < 1, sum a/(1 − r) from first term a.
- p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges iff p > 1. Harmonic series (p = 1) diverges.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** aₙ = (2n + 1)/(3n − 1) → 2/3 (divide by n). Converges to 2/3.

**Example 2.** Σ n/(n + 1) diverges since aₙ → 1 ≠ 0.

**Example 3.** Σ 3/2ⁿ (n ≥ 1) = 3·(1/2)/(1 − 1/2) = 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding convergence of Σaₙ just because aₙ → 0 (harmonic series counter-example).
- Using the geometric sum formula when |r| ≥ 1.
- Confusing the sequence limit with the series sum.

statements.s: Σ 1/n converges because 1/n → 0.
Σ 1/n² converges.
Σ (0.9)ⁿ converges.
If aₙ → 5, Σaₙ diverges.

quiz.why: Σ1/n^1.5 is a p-series with p = 1.5 > 1, so it converges.
This is a geometric series with first term 1 and ratio 1/3, so the sum is 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2.
(1 + 1/n)ⁿ → e as n → ∞. This is the standard definition of e.
The nth-term test says that if aₙ does not tend to 0 then the series diverges. But aₙ → 0 does not prove convergence, so it can prove divergence only.
Σ2ⁿ is a geometric series with common ratio r = 2 ≥ 1, so it diverges (its terms grow without limit).

lessons.title: Comparison, ratio, root and integral tests

scenes.text: Faced with Σ n²/3ⁿ, Pooja wonders which test to use.
Powers like 3ⁿ or factorials scream 'ratio test'.

steps.title: Tests for positive-term series
steps.body:
- **Limit comparison:** if aₙ/bₙ → finite non-zero l, Σaₙ and Σbₙ behave alike (pick bₙ = 1/nᵖ from leading powers).
- **D'Alembert ratio:** aₙ₊₁/aₙ → l: l < 1 converges, l > 1 diverges, l = 1 test fails.
- **Cauchy root:** (aₙ)^(1/n) → l, same conclusion.
- **Integral test:** f positive decreasing, Σf(n) and ∫₁^∞ f(x)dx converge together.
- **Raabe's test** (when ratio gives 1): n(aₙ/aₙ₊₁ − 1) → k, k > 1 converges, k < 1 diverges.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ n²/3ⁿ: ratio = ((n+1)²/n²)(1/3) → 1/3 < 1 ⇒ converges.

**Example 2.** Σ (2n + 3)/(n³ + 1): compare with 1/n²; ratio → 2 ⇒ converges.

**Example 3.** Σ (n/(n + 1))^(n²): root test (n/(n+1))ⁿ → 1/e < 1 ⇒ converges.

**Example 4.** Σ 1/(n log n): ∫ dx/(x log x) = log log x → ∞ ⇒ diverges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Declaring convergence when the ratio limit equals 1.
- Using comparison with a series that goes the wrong way (larger divergent series proves nothing).
- Forgetting the integral test needs f decreasing.

activity.prompt: Best first test

quiz.why: By the ratio test, if the limit of aₙ₊₁/aₙ is l < 1, the series converges. Here l = 1/2 < 1.
For large n, 1/(n² + n) behaves like 1/n². By comparison with the convergent Σ1/n² (p = 2), the series converges.
The ratio of consecutive terms of n!/10ⁿ is (n + 1)/10, which tends to infinity. Since l > 1, the series diverges.
For Σ1/n² the ratio (n/(n + 1))² → 1, so the ratio test is inconclusive. We need the p-series test instead.
Σ1/√n is a p-series with p = 1/2 ≤ 1, so it diverges.

scenes.text: 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converges to log 2, though 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges.
Convergence that depends on cancelling signs is called conditional.

steps.title: Leibniz test
steps.body:
Σ (−1)^(n+1) uₙ with uₙ > 0 converges if (i) uₙ ≥ uₙ₊₁ eventually and (ii) uₙ → 0.

**Absolute convergence:** Σ|aₙ| converges ⇒ Σaₙ converges. If Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| diverges, it is **conditionally** convergent.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ (−1)^(n+1)/n: uₙ = 1/n decreasing → 0 ⇒ converges; Σ1/n diverges ⇒ conditionally convergent.

**Example 2.** Σ (−1)ⁿ/n²: Σ1/n² converges ⇒ absolutely convergent.

**Example 3.** Σ (−1)ⁿ n/(n + 1): uₙ → 1 ≠ 0 ⇒ diverges (oscillates).

steps.title: Error bound
steps.body: For a Leibniz series, the error after stopping at term n is at most uₙ₊₁ — handy for 'how many terms for 3-decimal accuracy?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping the 'decreasing' check.
- Saying 'absolutely convergent' for the alternating harmonic series.
- Forgetting that absolute convergence implies convergence (not the reverse).

activity.prompt: Match series to behaviour

quiz.q: Leibniz test requires uₙ to be
quiz.why: The Leibniz (alternating series) test needs the terms uₙ to decrease and tend to 0.
The Leibniz test shows that Σ(−1)ⁿ/√n converges. But Σ1/√n diverges, so convergence is conditional, not absolute.
If a series converges absolutely (Σ|aₙ| converges), then it converges. The reverse is not always true.
ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − … converges at x = 1, so 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − … = ln 2 (log 2).

quiz.q: Terms needed so error < 0.01 in Σ(−1)^(n+1)/n
quiz.why: The error is less than the first neglected term. We need 1/(n + 1) < 0.01, so n is about 100.

lessons.title: Power series and radius of convergence

scenes.text: The series 1 + x + x² + … equals 1/(1 − x) — but only for |x| < 1.
Every power series has a radius inside which it converges.

steps.title: Radius of convergence
steps.body: For Σ aₙ xⁿ: R = lim |aₙ/aₙ₊₁| (if it exists) or 1/R = lim |aₙ|^(1/n). The series converges absolutely for |x| < R and diverges for |x| > R. Check the end points x = ±R separately.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Σ xⁿ/n: R = lim (n+1)/n = 1. At x = 1: harmonic (diverges); at x = −1: alternating harmonic (converges). Interval [−1, 1).

**Example 2.** Σ xⁿ/n!: R = lim (n + 1) = ∞ — converges for all x (it is eˣ).

**Example 3.** Σ n!xⁿ: R = lim 1/(n + 1) = 0 — converges only at x = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to test the end points.
- Inverting the ratio (using aₙ₊₁/aₙ for R).
- Confusing radius with interval.

activity.prompt: Radius of convergence of Σ xⁿ/3ⁿ

quiz.why: For Σxⁿ/n!, the ratio |x|/(n + 1) → 0 for every x, so the radius of convergence is infinite.
R = 1. At x = 1 the series is the harmonic series, which diverges, and at x = −1 it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges. So the interval is [−1, 1).
The ratio of coefficients (n + 1)/n → 1, so the radius of convergence of Σnxⁿ is 1.
For Σn!xⁿ the ratio (n + 1)|x| → ∞ for any x ≠ 0, so the radius is 0 and it converges only at x = 0.
Σ(2x)ⁿ is geometric in 2x and converges when |2x| < 1, i.e. |x| < 1/2.

questions.why: A p-series Σ1/nᵖ converges only when p > 1.

questions.why: 1/(n(n + 1)) = 1/n − 1/(n + 1). The series telescopes, so the sum is 1.

questions.why: The ratio of consecutive terms of Σ2ⁿ/n! is 2/(n + 1) → 0 < 1, so the series converges.

questions.why: By the root test the nth root of (n/(2n + 1))ⁿ is n/(2n + 1) → 1/2 < 1, so the series converges.

questions.why: By the integral test, ∫dx/(x ln²x) = −1/ln x converges, so the series converges.

questions.why: The total travel is a geometric series with first term 10 and ratio 0.8: 10/(1 − 0.8) = 50 cm.

questions.why: The first two equations are the same (the second is twice the first). With x = y, rank A = rank [A|B] = 2 < 3 unknowns, so there are infinitely many solutions.

questions.why: Multiply A² − 5A + 6I = 0 by A⁻¹: A − 5I + 6A⁻¹ = 0, so A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/6.

questions.why: y₁ = m y/√(1 − x²), so √(1 − x²)y₁ = my. Differentiating gives (1 − x²)y₂ − xy₁ = m√(1 − x²) y₁ = m²y.
