steps.title: Harmonic functions
steps.body: u is harmonic if uₓₓ + u_yy = 0. Real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic; v is the **harmonic conjugate** of u. The families u = c₁ and v = c₂ are orthogonal.

steps.title: Finding v and f
steps.body:
**Via CR:** dv = vₓdx + v_ydy = −u_y dx + uₓ dy; integrate (exact differential).
**Milne-Thomson:** f′(z) = uₓ(z, 0) − iu_y(z, 0). Integrate in z: f(z) = ∫[uₓ(z,0) − iu_y(z,0)]dz + C.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u = x² − y² + x. Harmonic: 2 − 2 = 0 ✔. uₓ = 2x + 1, u_y = −2y.
Milne-Thomson: f′ = (2z + 1) − i(0) ⇒ f = z² + z + C. So v = 2xy + y.

**Example 2.** u = eˣ cos y: uₓ = eˣ cos y, u_y = −eˣ sin y. f′ = e^z − i·0 ⇒ f = e^z + C, v = eˣ sin y.

**Example 3.** Given v = 2xy (imaginary part), use f′ = v_y(z,0) + ivₓ(z,0) = 2z + 0 ⇒ f = z² + C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting x = z, y = 0 before differentiating (differentiate first).
- Missing the minus sign in uₓ − iu_y.
- Not checking that u is harmonic first.

activity.prompt: Milne-Thomson steps (u given)
items: Check uₓₓ + u_yy = 0
Compute uₓ and u_y
Replace x by z and y by 0 in both
Form f′(z) = uₓ(z,0) − iu_y(z,0)
Integrate to get f(z) + C

quiz.why: u = x² − y² has u_xx + u_yy = 2 − 2 = 0, so it is harmonic (it is the real part of z²).
u = x is the real part of f(z) = z, so the harmonic conjugate is v = y.
u_xx + u_yy = 2 + 2 = 4 ≠ 0, so u = x² + y² is not harmonic.

quiz.q: Level curves u = c₁, v = c₂ of an analytic f are
quiz.why: For an analytic function, the curves u = c₁ and v = c₂ intersect at right angles (orthogonal), by the CR equations.
By the Milne-Thomson method, f′(z) = u_x(z, 0) − i u_y(z, 0), which is then integrated.

scenes.text: Electrostatics in an awkward region can be mapped to a simple strip or half-plane.
Analytic maps preserve angles — that is what 'conformal' means.

steps.title: Conformal maps
steps.body:
w = f(z) is conformal at z₀ if f is analytic and f′(z₀) ≠ 0: angles (magnitude and sense) between curves are preserved.
- w = z + c: translation
- w = az: rotation by arg a and magnification |a|
- w = 1/z: inversion + reflection
- w = z²: doubles angles at origin (not conformal at 0)

steps.title: Bilinear (Möbius) transformation
steps.body:
w = (az + b)/(cz + d), ad − bc ≠ 0. Maps circles/lines to circles/lines. Determined uniquely by three point images, using the cross-ratio:
(w − w₁)(w₂ − w₃)/[(w − w₃)(w₂ − w₁)] = (z − z₁)(z₂ − z₃)/[(z − z₃)(z₂ − z₁)].
Fixed points: solve z = (az + b)/(cz + d).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Fixed points of w = (z − 1)/(z + 1): z² + z = z − 1 ⇒ z² = −1 ⇒ z = ±i.

**Example 2.** Image of |z| = 2 under w = 1/z: |w| = 1/2 (circle radius ½).

**Example 3.** Bilinear map sending z = 0, 1, ∞ to w = −1, 0, 1: try w = (z − 1)/(z + 1): z = 0 → −1 ✔, z = 1 → 0 ✔, z → ∞ → 1 ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling w = z² conformal at z = 0 (f′(0) = 0).
- Forgetting the condition ad − bc ≠ 0.
- Arithmetic slips in the cross-ratio order.

activity.prompt: Match the mapping

quiz.why: A mapping is conformal (angle preserving) where f is analytic and f′(z) ≠ 0.
Under w = 1/z, |w| = 1/|z|. So |z| = 3 maps to the circle |w| = 1/3.
Fixed points satisfy z = (z − 1)/(z + 1), so z² + z = z − 1, i.e. z² = −1 and z = ±i.

quiz.q: A bilinear map is fixed by images of
quiz.why: A bilinear transformation has three free parameters, so it is determined by the images of three distinct points (cross-ratio).

quiz.q: w = z² is NOT conformal at
quiz.why: w = z² has f′(z) = 2z, which is 0 at z = 0, so the mapping is not conformal there.

scenes.text: AC engineers write voltages as V e^(jωt) because multiplication by e^(jθ) is rotation.
Understanding e^z, log z and powers in the complex plane makes phasors natural.

steps.title: Exponential, trig and log
steps.body:
- e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y); periodic with period 2πi.
- sin z = (e^(iz) − e^(−iz))/(2i), cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(−iz))/2; |sin z| can exceed 1.
- log z = ln|z| + i(arg z + 2nπ); principal value Log z uses −π < arg z ≤ π.
- z^c = e^(c log z).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** e^(iπ) = −1 (Euler's identity).

**Example 2.** Log(−1) = ln 1 + iπ = iπ.

**Example 3.** iⁱ = e^(i log i) = e^(i·iπ/2) = e^(−π/2) ≈ 0.208 (principal value — a real number!).

**Example 4.** Solve cos z = 2: e^(iz) + e^(−iz) = 4 ⇒ e^(iz) = 2 ± √3 ⇒ z = 2nπ − i ln(2 ± √3).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming |sin z| ≤ 1 for complex z.
- Treating log z as single-valued.
- Forgetting the 2nπ in general solutions.

activity.prompt: Values
activity.text: e^(iπ/2) = ___ and the principal value of Log(i) = iπ/___.

quiz.why: By Euler's formula e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = −1.
e^(z + 2πi) = e^z e^(2πi) = e^z, so e^z is periodic with period 2πi.
iⁱ = e^(i log i) = e^(i · iπ/2) = e^(−π/2), a real number.
The principal logarithm of −1 is ln|−1| + i Arg(−1) = 0 + iπ = iπ.
Yes: for z = iy, cos(iy) = cosh y, which can be larger than 1. Real cosine is bounded by 1, but complex cosine is not.

questions.q: f(z) = u + iv is analytic ⇒ u and v satisfy
questions.why: If f = u + iv is analytic, u and v satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations (a necessary condition).

questions.q: Which is not analytic anywhere?
questions.why: f(z) = z̄ = x − iy has u_x = 1 but v_y = −1, so the CR equations fail everywhere. It is nowhere analytic.

questions.q: Harmonic function satisfies
questions.why: A harmonic function satisfies Laplace's equation, u_xx + u_yy = 0.

questions.q: Real part of e^z
questions.why: e^z = eˣ(cos y + i sin y), so the real part is eˣ cos y.

questions.q: f = x² − y² + 2ixy equals
questions.why: (x + iy)² = x² − y² + 2ixy, so the expression is z².

questions.q: Harmonic conjugate of u = 2x(1 − y)
questions.why: By Milne-Thomson, f(z) = 2z + iz², which gives v = 2y + x² − y² (up to a constant).

questions.q: Assertion (A): f(z) = z̄ is not analytic.  Reason (R): CR equations fail: uₓ = 1 while v_y = −1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: for z̄, u = x and v = −y, so u_x = 1 but v_y = −1. The CR equations fail, which is why z̄ is not analytic.

questions.q: Fixed points of w = (3z − 4)/(z − 1)
questions.why: Fixed points satisfy z(z − 1) = 3z − 4, so z² − 4z + 4 = 0, giving the double root z = 2.

questions.q: Image of the line Re z = 1 under w = z + 2
questions.why: w = z + 2 is a translation by 2 to the right, so the line Re z = 1 goes to Re w = 3.

questions.q: If u = eˣ(x cos y − y sin y), Milne-Thomson gives f(z) =
questions.why: u_x(z, 0) = e^z(z + 1) (putting x = z, y = 0), and u_y(z, 0) = 0. So f′ = (z + 1)e^z and f = ze^z + C.

questions.q: Value of k for which u = x³ + kxy² is harmonic
questions.why: u_xx + u_yy = 6x + 2kx = 0 requires k = −3.

questions.q: Case: A potential φ = x² − y² in 2-D flow. The stream function ψ (harmonic conjugate) is
questions.why: φ = x² − y² is the real part of z², so the harmonic conjugate (stream function) is ψ = 2xy.

questions.q: Principal value of (1 + i)^i involves magnitude
questions.why: (1 + i)^i = exp(i ln(1 + i)) = exp(i(ln√2 + iπ/4)) = e^(−π/4) e^(i ln√2), so the magnitude is e^(−π/4).

questions.q: Mapping w = z² doubles angles at
questions.why: w = z² has derivative 2z, which is zero only at z = 0, so angles are not preserved at 0 (they are doubled there).

questions.q: Bilinear transformation mapping z = 1, i, −1 to w = 0, 1, ∞
questions.why: A bilinear map taking z = 1 to 0 and z = −1 to ∞ has the form w = k(z − 1)/(z + 1). With z = i → 1, k·i = 1, so k = −i.

questions.q: Solution of e^z = 1
questions.why: e^z = 1 requires the real part x = 0 and y = 2nπ, so z = 2nπi.

courses.title: Maths III · Unit 2 · Complex integration and residues
courses.summary: Contour integrals, Cauchy's integral theorem and formula, Taylor and Laurent series, singularities, residue theorem and evaluation of real definite integrals.
outcomes: Evaluate contour integrals directly and with Cauchy's theorem/formula
Expand functions in Taylor and Laurent series
Classify singularities and compute residues
Evaluate real integrals by contour integration
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A field engineer integrates a complex potential around a closed loop and gets zero.
Cauchy's theorem says that happens whenever no singularity is inside.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
**Contour integral:** ∫_C f(z)dz with z(t): ∫f(z(t))z′(t)dt. Key: ∮_(|z−a|=r) dz/(z − a) = 2πi; ∮(z − a)ⁿdz = 0 for integer n ≠ −1.
**Cauchy's theorem:** f analytic on and inside simple closed C ⇒ ∮_C f dz = 0.
**Cauchy's integral formula:** f(a) = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a) dz, and f⁽ⁿ⁾(a) = (n!/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − a)^(n+1) dz.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∮_(|z|=2) e^z/(z − 1) dz = 2πi·e¹ = 2πie.

**Example 2.** ∮_(|z|=1) e^(2z)/z³ dz: f = e^(2z), n = 2: (2πi/2!)f″(0) = πi·4 = 4πi.

**Example 3.** ∮_(|z|=3) dz/((z − 1)(z − 2)): partial fractions 1/(z − 2) − 1/(z − 1): 2πi − 2πi = 0.

**Example 4.** ∮_(|z|=1) cos z/(z − 2) dz = 0 (z = 2 is outside).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the formula when the point a is outside C (answer is 0).
- Forgetting n! in the derivative formula.
- Not checking which singular points lie inside the contour.

activity.prompt: ∮ over |z| = 1 of dz/z, divided by πi, equals?

quiz.why: z² is analytic inside and on the unit circle, so by Cauchy's theorem the integral is 0.
The point z = 1 lies inside |z| = 2, so by Cauchy's integral formula the integral is 2πi.
The point z = 3 lies outside |z| = 1, so the integrand is analytic inside and the integral is 0.
Cauchy's integral formula says f(a) = (1/2πi)∮f(z)/(z − a)dz.
By Cauchy's formula for derivatives, ∮sin z/z² dz = 2πi f′(0) with f = sin z, so f′(0) = cos 0 = 1 and the integral is 2πi.

scenes.text: Near a resonance, a circuit's transfer function blows up like 1/(s − p).
Laurent series capture that behaviour with negative powers.

steps.title: Series
steps.body:
**Taylor:** f analytic in |z − a| < R ⇒ f = Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(z − a)ⁿ/n!.
**Laurent:** in an annulus r < |z − a| < R, f = Σ aₙ(z − a)ⁿ + Σ bₙ(z − a)^(−n). The negative-power part is the principal part.

steps.title: Singularities
steps.body:
- **Removable:** no principal part (sin z/z at 0).
- **Pole of order m:** principal part ends at (z − a)^(−m).
- **Essential:** infinitely many negative powers (e^(1/z) at 0).
- Zeros: f(a) = 0; 1/f has a pole where f has a zero of the same order.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1/((z − 1)(z − 2)) for 1 < |z| < 2: = 1/(z − 2) − 1/(z − 1) = −(1/2)Σ(z/2)ⁿ − (1/z)Σ(1/z)ⁿ.

**Example 2.** e^(1/z) = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2!z²) + … — essential singularity at 0.

**Example 3.** (1 − cos z)/z² = 1/2 − z²/24 + … — removable singularity at 0.

**Example 4.** f = 1/(z²(z − 1)) has a pole of order 2 at 0 and a simple pole at 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expanding in the wrong region (|z| < 1 vs |z| > 1 give different series).
- Calling a removable singularity a pole.
- Missing the order of a pole by not factoring fully.

activity.prompt: Classify the singularity at z = 0

quiz.why: The Laurent series of e^(1/z) has infinitely many negative powers of z, so z = 0 is an essential singularity.
1/(z − 2)³ has the factor (z − 2) to the power 3 in the denominator, so it is a pole of order 3.
sin z/z → 1 as z → 0, so the singularity is removable.
A Laurent series is valid in an annulus (a ring-shaped region) between singularities.
The principal part of a Laurent series is the part containing negative powers of (z − a).

scenes.text: In control theory, inverse transforms are computed by summing residues at poles.
Residue theorem: ∮f dz = 2πi × (sum of residues inside).

steps.title: Computing residues
steps.body:
Residue = b₁, the coefficient of 1/(z − a).
- Simple pole: Res = lim (z − a)f(z); if f = p/q with q(a) = 0, q′(a) ≠ 0: Res = p(a)/q′(a).
- Pole of order m: Res = [1/(m − 1)!] lim d^(m−1)/dz^(m−1) [(z − a)^m f(z)].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/(m − 1)! factor.
- Including poles outside the contour.
- Using p/q′ for higher-order poles.

activity.prompt: Residue of 1/(z(z + 2)) at z = 0

quiz.why: The residue is the coefficient of 1/(z − 3) in the Laurent series. Here it is 1.
e^z/z has a simple pole at 0, and the residue is the value of e^z there: e⁰ = 1.
By the residue theorem, ∮f dz = 2πi × (sum of residues inside the contour).
cot z = cos z/sin z has a simple pole at 0 with residue cos 0/cos 0 = 1.
1/z³ has no 1/z term in its Laurent series, so its residue at 0 is 0.

scenes.text: Signal energy integrals like ∫ dx/(1 + x²) appear everywhere.
Closing the contour in the complex plane turns them into residue sums.

steps.title: Two standard types
steps.body:
**Type 1:** ∫₀^(2π) F(cos θ, sin θ)dθ. Put z = e^(iθ): cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2, sin θ = (z − 1/z)/(2i), dθ = dz/(iz); integrate over |z| = 1.
**Type 2:** ∫₋∞^∞ P(x)/Q(x)dx with deg Q ≥ deg P + 2 and no real roots of Q: = 2πi × Σ residues in the upper half-plane.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(2 + cos θ). With z: ∮ 2dz/(i(z² + 4z + 1)). Roots −2 ± √3; inside: −2 + √3. Res of 2/(i(z² + 4z + 1)) there = 2/(i·2√3). Integral = 2πi·1/(i√3) = 2π/√3.

**Example 2.** ∫₋∞^∞ dx/(1 + x²) = 2πi·Res at i of 1/(z² + 1) = 2πi/(2i) = π.

**Example 3.** ∫₋∞^∞ dx/(x² + 1)²: Res at i (order 2) = d/dz[(z + i)^(−2)] at i = −2/(2i)³ = 1/(4i) ⇒ π/2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including lower half-plane poles in Type 2.
- Errors in substituting dθ = dz/(iz).
- Forgetting the degree condition (needed for the semicircle contribution to vanish).

activity.prompt: Steps for ∫₀^(2π) F(cos θ, sin θ) dθ
items: Substitute z = e^(iθ)
Replace cos θ, sin θ and dθ in terms of z
Simplify to a rational function of z
Find poles inside |z| = 1 and their residues
Multiply the sum by 2πi

quiz.why: ∫₋∞^∞ dx/(x² + 1) = 2πi × Res at z = i = 2πi × 1/(2i) = π.
For integrals over 0 to 2π of trigonometric functions, put z = e^(iθ), turning it into a contour integral on the unit circle.
With z = e^(iθ), dz = i e^(iθ) dθ = iz dθ, so dθ = dz/(iz).
For real-line integrals closed by a large semicircle in the upper half-plane, only poles in the upper half-plane are counted.
Using z = e^(iθ), the integral becomes a contour integral, with the pole inside the unit circle at z = −2 + √3. The result is 2π/√3.

questions.why: ∮dz/z = 2πi, since the residue at the pole z = 0 inside the circle is 1.

questions.q: Cauchy's theorem applies when f is
questions.why: Cauchy's theorem needs f to be analytic on and inside the closed contour C.

questions.q: Residue of 1/(z + 1) at −1
questions.why: 1/(z + 1) has a simple pole at −1 with residue 1.
By Cauchy's formula with f(z) = z: ∮z/(z − 1)dz = 2πi f(1) = 2πi, since the point 1 is inside |z| = 2.

questions.q: Singularity of 1/sin z at 0
questions.why: sin z has a simple zero at 0, so 1/sin z has a simple pole there.

questions.q: Residue of z²/(z − 2) at 2
questions.why: For a simple pole the residue is the numerator evaluated at the pole: z² at 2 is 4.

questions.q: ∮_(|z|=1) e^z/z² dz
questions.why: By Cauchy's formula for derivatives, ∮e^z/z² dz = 2πi f′(0) with f = e^z, f′(0) = 1, so the integral is 2πi.

questions.q: Assertion (A): ∮_(|z|=1) dz/(z − 2) = 0.  Reason (R): z = 2 lies outside |z| = 1, so the integrand is analytic inside.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: the pole z = 2 lies outside |z| = 1, so the integrand is analytic inside the contour and Cauchy's theorem gives 0.

questions.q: Residue of 1/(z²(z − 1)) at 0
questions.why: For a double pole at 0 the residue is d/dz[1/(z − 1)] at 0 = −1/(z − 1)² = −1.
The poles ±1 are both inside |z| = 3 with residues 1/2 and −1/2, which add to 0, so the integral is 0.
The pole in the upper half-plane is z = 2i with residue 1/(4i). So the integral is 2πi/(4i) = π/2.

questions.q: Case: A transfer function H(z) = 1/(z(z − 0.5)). ∮_(|z|=1) H dz =
questions.why: The poles at z = 0 and z = 0.5 are both inside the unit circle. Residues are 1/(0 − 0.5) = −2 and 1/0.5 = 2. The sum is 0, so the integral is 0.
The pole of order 2 at i gives residue 1/(4i), so the integral is 2πi/(4i) = π/2 (a standard worked example).

questions.q: ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(5 + 4 cos θ)
questions.why: ∫₀^(2π) dθ/(a + b cos θ) = 2π/√(a² − b²) for a > |b|. With a = 5, b = 4: 2π/3.

questions.q: Laurent series of 1/(z(1 − z)) in 0 < |z| < 1 starts
questions.why: 1/(z(1 − z)) = (1/z)(1 + z + z² + …) for |z| < 1, so it begins 1/z + 1 + z + ….

courses.title: Maths III · Unit 3 · Partial differential equations and applications
courses.summary: Formation of PDEs, Lagrange's linear equation, homogeneous linear PDEs with constant coefficients, separation of variables, and the one-dimensional wave and heat equations and Laplace's equation.
outcomes: Form PDEs by eliminating constants or functions
Solve Lagrange's equation Pp + Qq = R
Find CF and PI for linear PDEs with constant coefficients
Solve wave, heat and Laplace equations by separation of variables
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Formation of PDEs and Lagrange's linear equation

scenes.text: A family of spheres z² + (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² can be described by one PDE.
Eliminating constants or arbitrary functions forms the PDE.

steps.title: Formation and notation
steps.body:
p = ∂z/∂x, q = ∂z/∂y, r = zₓₓ, s = zₓᵧ, t = z_yy.
- Eliminate arbitrary constants: differentiate w.r.t. x and y and eliminate.
- Eliminate arbitrary functions: e.g. z = f(x² + y²) ⇒ p = 2x f′, q = 2y f′ ⇒ yp − xq = 0.

steps.title: Lagrange's equation Pp + Qq = R
steps.body: Auxiliary equations dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R. Find two independent integrals u = c₁, v = c₂. General solution φ(u, v) = 0. Use grouping or multipliers (l, m, n) with lP + mQ + nR = 0.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** z = ax + by + ab: p = a, q = b ⇒ z = px + qy + pq.

**Example 2.** xp + yq = z: dx/x = dy/y = dz/z ⇒ y/x = c₁, z/x = c₂ ⇒ φ(y/x, z/x) = 0.

**Example 3.** (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y. Multipliers 1,1,1: d(x + y + z) = 0 ⇒ x + y + z = c₁. Multipliers x, y, z: x dx + y dy + z dz = 0 ⇒ x² + y² + z² = c₂. Solution φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Only one integral found — Lagrange needs two independent ones.
- Treating p, q as total derivatives.
- Not checking that multipliers make the denominator zero.

activity.prompt: Match the PDE notation

quiz.q: Eliminating f from z = f(x + y)
quiz.why: For z = f(x + y), p = f′ and q = f′, so p = q. This eliminates f.

quiz.q: Auxiliary equations of Pp + Qq = R
quiz.why: For Lagrange's equation Pp + Qq = R, the auxiliary equations are dx/P = dy/Q = dz/R.
If u and v are two independent integrals of the auxiliary equations, the general solution is φ(u, v) = 0 for an arbitrary function φ.
The auxiliary equations dx/1 = dy/1 = dz/1 give x − y = c₁ and z − x = c₂, so the general solution is φ(x − y, z − x) = 0.

quiz.q: Order of z = ax + by eliminated PDE
quiz.why: Eliminating the two constants a and b from z = ax + by gives a first-order PDE: z = px + qy.

scenes.text: A drumhead's shape satisfies a second-order linear PDE.
Just like ODEs: CF from an auxiliary equation, PI from operator rules.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
With D = ∂/∂x, D′ = ∂/∂y, f(D, D′)z = F(x, y).
Auxiliary equation: put D = m, D′ = 1.
- Distinct roots m₁, m₂: CF = f₁(y + m₁x) + f₂(y + m₂x)
- Repeated m: CF = f₁(y + mx) + x f₂(y + mx)

steps.title: Particular integrals
steps.body:
- F = e^(ax + by): PI = e^(ax + by)/f(a, b) if f(a, b) ≠ 0.
- F = sin(ax + by) or cos: replace D² → −a², DD′ → −ab, D′² → −b².
- F = xᵐyⁿ: expand 1/f(D, D′) in series.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** (D² − 5DD′ + 6D′²)z = 0: m² − 5m + 6 = 0 ⇒ m = 2, 3 ⇒ z = f₁(y + 2x) + f₂(y + 3x).

**Example 2.** (D² − 2DD′ + D′²)z = e^(x + 2y): CF = f₁(y + x) + xf₂(y + x); PI = e^(x + 2y)/(1 − 4 + 4) = e^(x + 2y).

**Example 3.** (D² + DD′)z = sin(x + y)? Replace: −1 + (−1) = −2 ⇒ PI = −½ sin(x + y).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing f(y − mx) instead of f(y + mx) with this convention.
- Forgetting the x multiplier for repeated roots.
- Replacing D with a and D′ with b inconsistently.

activity.prompt: CF of (D² − D′²)z = 0
activity.text: Roots m = ±1, so z = f₁(y + x) + f₂(y ___ x).

quiz.why: The auxiliary equation m² − 4m + 4 = 0 has a repeated root m = 2, so z = f₁(y + 2x) + x f₂(y + 2x).
PI = e^(x + y)/f(1, 1) with f = D² + D′² giving f(1, 1) = 2, so e^(x + y)/2.
Replace D by m and D′ by 1: 2m² + 5m + 2 = 0.
For cos(x + 2y), D² → −1 and D′² → −4, so D² − D′² → −1 + 4 = 3. PI = cos(x + 2y)/3.

quiz.q: Number of arbitrary functions in CF of second-order homogeneous PDE
quiz.why: The complementary function of a second-order homogeneous linear PDE contains 2 arbitrary functions.

lessons.title: Separation of variables: the wave equation

scenes.text: A string of length L fixed at both ends is plucked.
Its displacement obeys yₜₜ = c²yₓₓ; standing waves sin(nπx/L) are the modes.

steps.title: Solution
steps.body:
yₜₜ = c²yₓₓ, y(0,t) = y(L,t) = 0. Assume y = X(x)T(t): X″/X = T″/(c²T) = −k².
X = sin(nπx/L), T = Aₙcos(nπct/L) + Bₙsin(nπct/L).
y = Σ [Aₙcos(nπct/L) + Bₙsin(nπct/L)] sin(nπx/L).
Aₙ from y(x,0) = f(x): Aₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L f sin(nπx/L)dx; Bₙ from initial velocity g(x): Bₙ = (2/(nπc))∫₀^L g sin(nπx/L)dx.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** String released from rest with y(x,0) = 3 sin(πx/L): only A₁ = 3 ⇒ y = 3 sin(πx/L) cos(πct/L).

**Example 2.** y(x,0) = sin³(πx/L) = (3/4)sin(πx/L) − (1/4)sin(3πx/L), at rest ⇒ y = (3/4)sin(πx/L)cos(πct/L) − (1/4)sin(3πx/L)cos(3πct/L).

Natural frequencies fₙ = nc/(2L) — the musical harmonics.

steps.title: Why −k²?
steps.body: Choosing the separation constant negative gives oscillating X that can vanish at both ends; positive or zero constants give only the trivial solution with these boundary conditions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a positive separation constant for fixed ends.
- Missing the nπc/L factor in Bₙ.
- Forgetting to use identities like sin³θ before matching coefficients.

activity.prompt: String L = 0.5 m, wave speed c = 200 m/s. Fundamental frequency c/(2L) in Hz?

quiz.why: The one-dimensional wave equation is y_tt = c² y_xx.
For a string fixed at both ends, X(0) = X(L) = 0, so the spatial mode shapes are sin(nπx/L).
Zero initial velocity (released from rest) means y_t(x, 0) = 0, which makes the Bₙ coefficients zero.
With ωₙ = nπc/L, the frequency in cycles per second is fₙ = nc/(2L).
Separating variables gives X″ + k²X = 0 for oscillatory modes, so the separation constant is −k² (negative).

scenes.text: A rod whose ends are kept at 0 °C cools from an initial profile.
Each mode decays like e^(−c²n²π²t/L²) — higher modes vanish fastest.

steps.title: Heat equation uₜ = c²uₓₓ
steps.body:
Ends at 0: u = Σ bₙ e^(−c²n²π²t/L²) sin(nπx/L), bₙ = (2/L)∫₀^L u(x,0) sin(nπx/L)dx.
Steady state (t → ∞): uₓₓ = 0 ⇒ linear profile between end temperatures.

steps.title: Laplace's equation (2-D steady state)
steps.body:
uₓₓ + u_yy = 0 on a rectangle 0 < x < a, 0 < y < b with u = 0 on three sides and u = f(x) on y = b:
u = Σ cₙ sin(nπx/a) sinh(nπy/a), cₙ sinh(nπb/a) = (2/a)∫₀^a f sin(nπx/a)dx.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** u(x,0) = 5 sin(πx/L), ends at 0: u = 5 e^(−c²π²t/L²) sin(πx/L).

**Example 2.** Rod 0 ≤ x ≤ 10 with ends held at 20 °C and 80 °C: steady state u = 20 + 6x.

**Example 3.** Ends change suddenly: write u = u_s(x) + v(x,t) with v satisfying zero end conditions, then solve for v by the series above.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cos(…t) in the heat equation (it decays exponentially, not oscillates).
- Forgetting the steady-state part when end temperatures are non-zero.
- Using sinh vs sin in the wrong variable for Laplace problems.

activity.prompt: Which equation?

quiz.why: In the heat equation the time factor is e^(−λt), so each mode decays exponentially.

quiz.q: Steady-state temperature in a rod satisfies
quiz.why: At steady state u_t = 0, so the heat equation reduces to u_xx = 0, which gives a linear temperature profile.

quiz.q: Rod ends at 0 °C and 100 °C, length 1. Steady u(0.25)
quiz.why: The steady state is linear: u = 100x between 0 °C at x = 0 and 100 °C at x = 1. At x = 0.25, u = 25 °C.
Each mode decays at rate proportional to n², so the highest-n mode decays fastest.
Laplace's equation has no time derivative, so it describes steady-state potential or temperature.

questions.q: p denotes
questions.why: In standard PDE notation, p = ∂z/∂x and q = ∂z/∂y (r, s, t are the second derivatives).

questions.q: Heat equation is
questions.why: The one-dimensional heat equation is u_t = c²u_xx.

questions.q: Laplace's equation in 2-D
questions.why: Laplace's equation in two dimensions is u_xx + u_yy = 0.

questions.q: Eliminating a, b from z = (x + a)(y + b)
questions.why: From z = (x + a)(y + b): p = y + b and q = x + a, so pq = (x + a)(y + b) = z.

questions.q: Solution of xp + yq = 3z
questions.why: The auxiliary equations dx/x = dy/y = dz/(3z) give y/x = c₁ and z/x³ = c₂, so φ(y/x, z/x³) = 0.

questions.q: CF of (D² − 3DD′ + 2D′²)z = 0
questions.why: m² − 3m + 2 = 0 gives m = 1, 2, so z = f₁(y + x) + f₂(y + 2x).

questions.q: PI of (D² − DD′)z = e^(2x + y)
Assertion (A): For a string fixed at both ends the separation constant must be negative.  Reason (R): Only then can X(x) vanish at both ends without being identically zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: with a positive separation constant X would be exponential or hyperbolic and cannot vanish at both ends (except trivially), so only a negative constant, giving sine modes, works.

questions.q: Case: A 1 m rod has ends held at 0 °C and 50 °C. Steady temperature at x = 0.4 m
questions.why: With fixed ends the steady state is linear: u = 50x. At x = 0.4, u = 20 °C.

questions.q: String y(x,0) = 2 sin(2πx/L), at rest. Solution
questions.why: The initial shape is the single mode n = 2, and the string starts at rest, so y = 2 sin(2πx/L) cos(2πct/L).

questions.q: Heat problem u(x,0) = 4 sin(3πx/L): u =
questions.why: Mode 3 has λ = (3πc/L)² = 9π²c²/L², so u = 4e^(−9π²c²t/L²) sin(3πx/L).

questions.q: Solution of (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y
questions.why: The multipliers (1, 1, 1) and (x, y, z) give d(x + y + z) = 0 and d(x² + y² + z²) = 0, so φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0.
options: φ(x + y + z, x² + y² + z²) = 0

questions.q: Ratio of decay rates of mode 2 to mode 1 in heat equation
questions.why: Decay rates are proportional to n², so mode 2 decays 4 times faster than mode 1.

questions.q: Classify uₓₓ + 4uₓᵧ + 4u_yy = 0 (B² − 4AC)
questions.why: A = 1, B = 4, C = 4, so B² − 4AC = 16 − 16 = 0, which means the equation is parabolic.

questions.q: Classify the wave equation
questions.why: For y_tt − c²y_xx = 0, B² − 4AC = 4c² > 0, so it is hyperbolic.

courses.title: Maths III · Unit 4 · Probability and probability distributions
courses.summary: Axioms and conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, random variables, expectation and variance, and binomial, Poisson, normal and exponential distributions with engineering applications.
outcomes: Use conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
Work with discrete and continuous random variables
Apply binomial and Poisson distributions
Use the normal distribution with z-tables
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem

scenes.text: Three machines make 50%, 30%, 20% of chips with defect rates 2%, 3%, 5%.
A chip is defective. Which machine most likely made it? Bayes' theorem.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
- P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)
- Independent: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
- Total probability: P(D) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(D|Eᵢ)
- **Bayes:** P(Eᵢ|D) = P(Eᵢ)P(D|Eᵢ)/Σ P(Eⱼ)P(D|Eⱼ)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (chips).** P(D) = 0.5(0.02) + 0.3(0.03) + 0.2(0.05) = 0.010 + 0.009 + 0.010 = 0.029.
P(M₁|D) = 0.010/0.029 ≈ 0.345; P(M₂|D) ≈ 0.310; P(M₃|D) ≈ 0.345.

**Example 2.** Two dice: P(sum = 8) = 5/36. P(sum = 8 | first die is 3) = 1/6.

**Example 3.** A test is 99% sensitive, 95% specific, prevalence 1%. P(disease | positive) = 0.0099/(0.0099 + 0.0495) ≈ 0.167 — most positives are false alarms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A).
- Assuming mutually exclusive events are independent (they are not, unless one has probability 0).
- Forgetting to subtract the intersection in the union rule.

activity.prompt: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, independent. P(A ∪ B) = ?

quiz.why: Conditional probability is P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B).

quiz.q: Independent A, B with P = 0.3, 0.5: P(A ∩ B)
quiz.why: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.
Bayes' theorem updates a prior probability given evidence to give a posterior probability.

quiz.q: P(at least one head in 3 tosses)
quiz.why: P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no head) = 1 − (1/2)³ = 7/8.

quiz.q: Mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are
quiz.why: For mutually exclusive A and B with positive probabilities, P(A ∩ B) = 0, which is not equal to P(A)P(B) > 0, so they are dependent.

scenes.text: A machine breaks down 0, 1, 2 times a month with probabilities 0.6, 0.3, 0.1.
Expected breakdowns E(X) = 0.5 per month — plan the budget from that.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Discrete X: pmf p(x), Σp = 1, E(X) = Σx p(x), Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
Continuous X: pdf f(x) ≥ 0, ∫f = 1, E(X) = ∫x f dx, CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x).
E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b; Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Var = E(X²) − E(X)² (not E(X − 1)² or similar).
- Adding b to variance in Var(aX + b).
- Treating pdf values as probabilities (P(X = x) = 0 for continuous X).

activity.prompt: f(x) = kx on 0 < x < 2 is a pdf. k = ?

quiz.why: The probabilities of all values of a discrete random variable add to 1.
Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) = 4 × 4 = 16. Adding a constant does not change variance.
For a continuous variable, the probability at a single point is 0, since probability is the area under the density over an interval.

scenes.text: A batch has 10 items each defective with p = 0.1 — binomial.
A call centre gets 3 calls per minute on average — Poisson.

steps.title: Binomial B(n, p)
steps.body: P(X = r) = ⁿCᵣ pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ, q = 1 − p. Mean np, variance npq (variance < mean). Use when n independent trials, two outcomes, constant p.

steps.title: Poisson P(λ)
steps.body: P(X = r) = e^(−λ)λʳ/r!. Mean = variance = λ. Limit of binomial when n large, p small, np = λ. Recurrence: P(r + 1) = λP(r)/(r + 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using binomial when trials are not independent.
- Forgetting P(0) when computing 'at least 1' (use complement).
- Mixing up rate units (per minute vs per hour) in λ.

activity.prompt: Match the distribution facts

quiz.why: The mean of a binomial B(n, p) is np = 20 × 0.3 = 6.
For a Poisson distribution the mean and variance are both equal to λ.

quiz.q: Binomial with mean 4, variance 3 has p =
quiz.why: np = 4 and npq = 3 give q = 3/4, so p = 1/4.

scenes.text: Shaft diameters are normally distributed with mean 25.00 mm and σ = 0.02 mm.
What fraction falls outside 24.96–25.04 mm? Convert to z and read the table.

steps.title: Normal N(μ, σ²)
steps.body:
f(x) = [1/(σ√(2π))] e^(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)). Symmetric about μ; mean = median = mode.
Standardise z = (x − μ)/σ ⇒ Z ~ N(0,1).
Empirical rule: about 68.3% within 1σ, 95.4% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ.

steps.title: Exponential distribution
steps.body: f(x) = λe^(−λx), x ≥ 0. Mean 1/λ, variance 1/λ². P(X > t) = e^(−λt). **Memoryless:** P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). Models lifetimes and waiting times.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Shafts: limits are ±2σ ⇒ about 95.4% inside, ≈ 4.6% rejected.

**Example 2.** Marks N(60, 10²): P(X > 75) = P(Z > 1.5) = 0.5 − 0.4332 = 0.0668.

**Example 3.** Bulb life exponential, mean 1000 h: P(lasts > 1500 h) = e^(−1.5) ≈ 0.223.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using variance instead of σ in z = (x − μ)/σ.
- Reading the table area from 0 to z as the tail area.
- Forgetting the exponential mean is 1/λ (not λ).

bands.text: Far below the mean — under 2.3% of values are this low.
Within one σ of the mean — about 68% of values.

quiz.why: For a normal distribution about 68% of the area lies within one standard deviation of the mean (empirical rule).
The mean of an exponential distribution with rate λ is 1/λ = 1/0.5 = 2.
The exponential distribution is memoryless: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t).
The normal curve is symmetric about its mean μ.

questions.q: P(sure event)
questions.why: By the axioms, the probability of the sure (certain) event is 1.

questions.q: Mean of B(n, p)
questions.why: The mean of a binomial B(n, p) is np.

questions.q: Standard normal has mean and SD
questions.why: The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

questions.q: Two coins: P(both heads | at least one head)
questions.why: The sample space given at least one head has 3 outcomes (HH, HT, TH), and only HH is both. So the probability is 1/3, i.e. (1/4)/(3/4).

questions.q: Poisson λ = 1: P(X = 1)
E(X) for a fair die
Var of fair die roll
Assertion (A): Variance of a binomial distribution is less than its mean.  Reason (R): Variance = npq and q < 1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: variance npq is less than the mean np because q < 1, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Bayes case: Box A (2 red, 3 blue), Box B (4 red, 1 blue), box chosen at random, red drawn. P(Box A | red)
f(x) = 3x² on (0,1): E(X)
questions.why: E(X) = ∫₀¹ x · 3x² dx = 3∫x³dx = 3/4.

questions.q: Case: 1% of welds fail; 200 welds inspected. Poisson P(no failure)

questions.why: With σ = 4, 46 to 54 is μ ± 1σ, which has probability about 0.683.

questions.q: Exponential λ = 0.01/h: P(failure within 100 h)
questions.why: For an exponential distribution, P(X ≤ t) = 1 − e^(−λt) = 1 − e^(−0.01 × 100) = 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.632.

questions.q: For Poisson, if P(X = 1) = P(X = 2), λ =
questions.why: P(1) = λe^(−λ) and P(2) = λ²e^(−λ)/2. Setting them equal gives λ = λ²/2, so λ = 2.

questions.q: Binomial with n = 5, p = 0.5: P(X ≥ 4)

courses.title: Maths III · Unit 5 · Statistics: correlation, regression and testing
courses.summary: Measures of central tendency and dispersion, curve fitting by least squares, Karl Pearson and Spearman correlation, regression lines, and basics of sampling and hypothesis tests (z, t, chi-square).
outcomes: Compute mean, SD and coefficient of variation
Fit straight lines and parabolas by least squares
Find correlation and regression coefficients
Carry out simple z, t and chi-square tests
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Machine A fills bottles with mean 500 ml, SD 2 ml; machine B mean 500 ml, SD 6 ml.
Same average, very different consistency — dispersion matters.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body:
Mean x̄ = Σx/n; median (middle value); mode (most frequent).
Variance σ² = Σ(x − x̄)²/n = Σx²/n − x̄²; SD σ.
Coefficient of variation CV = (σ/x̄) × 100% — lower CV means more consistent.
Skewness (Karl Pearson) = (mean − mode)/σ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: x̄ = 40/8 = 5. Σx² = 4 + 48 + 50 + 49 + 81 = 232. σ² = 232/8 − 25 = 4 ⇒ σ = 2.

**Example 2.** Two batsmen: A mean 50, σ 10 (CV 20%); B mean 40, σ 4 (CV 10%) ⇒ B is more consistent, A scores more.

steps.title: Sample vs population
steps.body: For estimating a population variance from a sample use s² = Σ(x − x̄)²/(n − 1). Exams usually state which to use — read carefully.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by n − 1 when the question wants the population formula, or vice versa.
- Comparing consistency by SD when means differ (use CV).
- Forgetting to square the mean in Σx²/n − x̄².

activity.prompt: Data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — population variance?

quiz.why: The coefficient of variation is CV = (σ/x̄) × 100%.
A lower CV means less relative variation, so the data are more consistent.
Sorted: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The middle value is 5.
All values are equal, so there is no spread and the standard deviation is 0.

quiz.q: Adding 10 to every value changes SD by
quiz.why: Adding a constant to every value shifts the mean but leaves the spread unchanged, so SD does not change.

scenes.text: A thermistor's readings vs temperature look nearly linear.
Least squares gives the best straight line y = a + bx through scattered data.

steps.title: Normal equations
steps.body:
Line y = a + bx: Σy = na + bΣx; Σxy = aΣx + bΣx².
Parabola y = a + bx + cx²: add Σx²y = aΣx² + bΣx³ + cΣx⁴.
Exponential y = aeᵇˣ: take log: ln y = ln a + bx (fit a line to (x, ln y)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x: 1, 2, 3, 4; y: 3, 5, 7, 10. n = 4, Σx = 10, Σy = 25, Σx² = 30, Σxy = 3 + 10 + 21 + 40 = 74.
25 = 4a + 10b; 74 = 10a + 30b ⇒ multiply first by 2.5: 62.5 = 10a + 25b ⇒ 11.5 = 5b ⇒ b = 2.3, a = (25 − 23)/4 = 0.5. Line: y = 0.5 + 2.3x.

**Example 2.** Fitting y = axᵇ: log y = log a + b log x — linear in (log x, log y).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Arithmetic errors in Σxy (build a table).
- Fitting y = aeᵇˣ directly without the log transform.
- Using x̄, ȳ formulas incorrectly — the line always passes through (x̄, ȳ), use that to check.

activity.prompt: Least-squares straight-line procedure
items: Tabulate x, y, x², xy
Compute Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy
Write the two normal equations
Solve for a and b
Check the line passes through (x̄, ȳ)

quiz.why: The least-squares regression line passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ), from the first normal equation.

quiz.q: To fit y = aeᵇˣ we fit a line to
quiz.why: Taking logs, ln y = ln a + bx, which is linear in x, so we fit a line to (x, ln y).

quiz.q: Number of normal equations for a parabola
quiz.why: A parabola y = a + bx + cx² has 3 unknown coefficients, so there are 3 normal equations.
The method of least squares minimises the sum of the squared residuals (differences between observed and fitted values).

quiz.q: In Example 1, predicted y at x = 5
quiz.why: Using the fitted line from the worked example, the prediction at x = 5 comes to 12.

scenes.text: A teacher records hours studied and marks for 10 students.
r measures how strongly they move together; regression predicts marks from hours.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Karl Pearson r = Cov(x,y)/(σₓσ_y) = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy]/√{[nΣx² − (Σx)²][nΣy² − (Σy)²]}, −1 ≤ r ≤ 1.
Spearman rank: ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)).
Regression y on x: y − ȳ = b_yx(x − x̄), b_yx = rσ_y/σₓ. x on y: x − x̄ = b_xy(y − ȳ), b_xy = rσₓ/σ_y.
r² = b_yx·b_xy; r has the sign of the regression coefficients; lines meet at (x̄, ȳ).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Regression lines 8x − 10y + 66 = 0 and 40x − 18y = 214. Mean: solve ⇒ x̄ = 13, ȳ = 17.
Assume first is y on x: y = 0.8x + 6.6 ⇒ b_yx = 0.8; second x on y: x = 0.45y + 5.35 ⇒ b_xy = 0.45. r² = 0.36 ⇒ r = 0.6 (valid since ≤ 1).

**Example 2.** Ranks with d = 1, −1, 2, −2, 0 (n = 5): Σd² = 10 ⇒ ρ = 1 − 60/120 = 0.5.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assigning regression lines the wrong way round (check b_yx·b_xy ≤ 1).
- Assuming correlation means causation.
- Not averaging ranks for ties in Spearman's formula.

statements.s: r = −0.9 shows a strong negative linear relationship.
r = 0 means no relationship of any kind.
Both regression lines pass through (x̄, ȳ).
b_yx = 0.8 and b_xy = 1.5 is possible.

quiz.why: The correlation coefficient always lies between −1 and 1.
The square of the correlation coefficient equals the product of the two regression coefficients: r² = b_yx · b_xy.
r² = b_yx · b_xy = 0.4 × 0.9 = 0.36, so r = 0.6 (positive, since both coefficients are positive).
Spearman's ρ = 1 − 6Σd²/(n(n² − 1)). With Σd² = 0, ρ = 1, meaning perfect agreement in ranks.
The two regression lines coincide when the correlation is perfect, r = ±1.

scenes.text: A new alloy's sample mean strength is 520 MPa against the old 500 MPa.
Is the improvement real or chance? A hypothesis test decides at a chosen significance level.

steps.title: Framework
steps.body: H₀ (null, no difference) vs H₁. Significance level α (5% or 1%). Compute test statistic; compare with critical value. Type I error: reject true H₀ (probability α). Type II: accept false H₀.

steps.title: Common tests
steps.body:
- **Large-sample z (mean):** z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n); |z| > 1.96 ⇒ reject at 5% (two-tailed).
- **Small-sample t:** t = (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n), ν = n − 1 degrees of freedom.
- **Chi-square goodness of fit:** χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, ν = (classes − 1 − parameters estimated).
- **F-test** compares two variances: F = s₁²/s₂² (larger on top).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using z for small samples with unknown σ (use t).
- Wrong degrees of freedom.
- Saying H₀ is 'proved' — we only fail to reject it.

activity.prompt: Which test?

quiz.why: The critical value of |z| at the 5% level for a two-tailed test is 1.96.
A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis H₀.

quiz.q: Degrees of freedom of t-test with n = 15
quiz.why: For a one-sample t-test the degrees of freedom are n − 1 = 14.
The chi-square statistic is χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
If the computed |z| is less than the critical value, we do not reject H₀ (there is not enough evidence against it).

questions.q: Mean of 2, 4, 6, 8
Correlation coefficient lies in
questions.why: The correlation coefficient lies in [−1, 1].

questions.q: χ² test is used for
questions.why: The chi-square test is used for goodness of fit (and for independence in contingency tables).
The mean is 5 and the squared deviations sum to 32, so variance = 32/8 = 4 and SD = 2.

lessons.title: Roots of equations: bisection and Newton–Raphson

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**Bisection:** if f(a)f(b) < 0, take c = (a + b)/2 and keep the half with a sign change. Always converges; error halves each step.
**Newton–Raphson:** xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f′(xₙ). Quadratic convergence near a simple root; can fail if f′ ≈ 0.
**Regula falsi:** x = (af(b) − bf(a))/(f(b) − f(a)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting NR where f′(x₀) = 0.
- Not checking a sign change before bisection.
- Stopping too early — iterate until successive values agree to required decimals.

activity.prompt: Implement Newton–Raphson to find √10 starting from 3. Print the root rounded to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
def f(x):
    return x*x - 10

def df(x):
    return 2*x

x = 3.0
# iterate 5 times: x = x - f(x)/df(x)

print(round(x, 4))
activity.solution:
x = 3.0
for _ in range(5):
    x = x - (x*x - 10)/(2*x)
print(round(x, 4))
activity.hint: Use a for loop and update x with x - f(x)/df(x).

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Forward differences Δyᵢ = yᵢ₊₁ − yᵢ.
**Newton forward:** y = y₀ + pΔy₀ + p(p−1)Δ²y₀/2! + p(p−1)(p−2)Δ³y₀/3! + …, p = (x − x₀)/h. Use near the start of the table.
**Newton backward:** y = yₙ + p∇yₙ + p(p+1)∇²yₙ/2! + …, p = (x − xₙ)/h. Use near the end.
**Lagrange (unequal spacing):** y = Σ yᵢ Π_(j≠i) (x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ).

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: Rules (h = step, n intervals)
steps.body:
**Trapezoidal:** ∫ ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + yₙ + 2(y₁ + … + yₙ₋₁)]. Error O(h²).
**Simpson's 1/3 (n even):** (h/3)[y₀ + yₙ + 4(odd ordinates) + 2(even interior ordinates)]. Error O(h⁴); exact for cubics.
**Simpson's 3/8 (n multiple of 3):** (3h/8)[y₀ + yₙ + 3(y₁ + y₂ + y₄ + y₅ + …) + 2(y₃ + y₆ + …)].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Simpson 1/3 with an odd number of intervals.
- Counting ordinates instead of intervals (n + 1 ordinates for n intervals).
- Mixing up the weights 4 and 2.

activity.prompt: Write simpson(f, a, b, n) for Simpson's 1/3 rule and print the integral of 1/(1+x²) on [0,1] with n = 4, rounded to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    # add 4*f for odd i, 2*f for even i (1..n-1)
    return s * h / 3

print(round(simpson(lambda x: 1/(1+x*x), 0, 1, 4), 4))
activity.solution:
def simpson(f, a, b, n):
    h = (b - a) / n
    s = f(a) + f(b)
    for i in range(1, n):
        s += (4 if i % 2 else 2) * f(a + i*h)
    return s * h / 3

print(round(simpson(lambda x: 1/(1+x*x), 0, 1, 4), 4))
activity.hint: Loop i from 1 to n−1; weight 4 when i is odd, 2 when even.

quiz.why: Simpson's 1/3 rule takes the strips in pairs, so the number of intervals n must be even.

steps.title: ODE methods for y′ = f(x,y), y(x₀) = y₀
steps.body:
**Euler:** yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f(xₙ, yₙ) (error O(h)).
**Modified Euler (Heun):** predictor y* = yₙ + hf(xₙ,yₙ); corrector yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + (h/2)[f(xₙ,yₙ) + f(xₙ₊₁, y*)].
**RK4:** k₁ = hf(x, y), k₂ = hf(x + h/2, y + k₁/2), k₃ = hf(x + h/2, y + k₂/2), k₄ = hf(x + h, y + k₃); yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + (k₁ + 2k₂ + 2k₃ + k₄)/6.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using old values in Gauss–Seidel (that's Jacobi).
- Forgetting h inside the k's of RK4.
- Applying Gauss–Seidel to a system that is not diagonally dominant without rearranging.

activity.prompt: Use Euler's method with h = 0.1 for y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, and print y at x = 0.2 rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    # update y then x
    pass
print(round(y, 2))
activity.solution:
x, y, h = 0.0, 1.0, 0.1
for _ in range(2):
    y = y + h*(x + y)
    x = x + h
print(round(y, 2))
activity.hint: y_new = y + h*f(x, y), then advance x by h.

scenes.text: Meera sees rainbow bands on a soap bubble and on an oil film on the road.
Both are interference: light waves from two surfaces add or cancel.

steps.title: Conditions for sustained interference
steps.body:
- Sources must be **coherent** (constant phase difference) — obtained by dividing one wavefront (Young) or amplitude (thin films).
- Same wavelength, nearly equal amplitudes, and small path differences compared to the coherence length.
Path difference Δ and phase difference δ: δ = (2π/λ)Δ.

steps.title: Young's double slit
steps.body:
Slit separation d, screen distance D. Bright fringes: Δ = nλ ⇒ yₙ = nλD/d. Dark: Δ = (2n + 1)λ/2.
Fringe width β = λD/d. Intensity I = 4I₀cos²(δ/2).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** λ = 600 nm, d = 0.5 mm, D = 1 m: β = 600×10⁻⁹ × 1/(0.5×10⁻³) = 1.2 mm.

**Example 2.** In YDSE the 10th bright fringe is 6 mm from the centre with D = 1.2 m, d = 1 mm: λ = yd/(nD) = (6×10⁻³)(10⁻³)/(10 × 1.2) = 500 nm.

**Example 3.** A thin glass sheet (μ = 1.5, t = 6 µm) in one beam shifts the pattern by (μ − 1)tD/d — the shift equals (μ − 1)t/λ fringes = 0.5 × 6×10⁻⁶/600×10⁻⁹ = 5 fringes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using mm and m together without converting.
- Thinking two separate bulbs give a stable pattern (they are incoherent).
- Forgetting that the sheet shifts the pattern towards the covered slit.

activity.prompt: YDSE: λ = 500 nm, d = 0.25 mm, D = 1 m. Fringe width in mm?

quiz.why: The fringe width in Young's experiment is β = λD/d.
Coherent sources emit waves with a constant phase difference, which is needed for stable interference.

quiz.q: If d is doubled, β becomes
quiz.why: β = λD/d, so if the slit separation d is doubled, the fringe width halves.
Dark fringes occur where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths: Δ = (2n + 1)λ/2 (destructive interference).

quiz.q: Interference in thin films is by division of
quiz.why: In thin films the wave is split into reflected and transmitted parts by partial reflection, which divides its amplitude, so it is interference by division of amplitude.

scenes.text: Spectacle lenses look slightly purple — they carry an anti-reflection coating.
A film λ/4 thick makes reflected waves cancel.

steps.title: Reflected light from a film
steps.body:
Film of thickness t, index μ, refraction angle r. Path difference 2μt cos r, plus λ/2 phase change on reflection from the denser medium.
Reflected: dark when 2μt cos r = nλ; bright when 2μt cos r = (2n + 1)λ/2. (Conditions swap in transmitted light.)
Wedge film: fringe width β = λ/(2μθ).

steps.title: Newton's rings
steps.body:
Plano-convex lens (radius R) on glass; air film t = r²/(2R).
Reflected light, centre dark. Dark ring n: Dₙ² = 4nλR/μ. Bright ring: Dₙ² = 2(2n − 1)λR/μ.
Wavelength from two rings: λ = (D²ₙ₊ₚ − D²ₙ)/(4pR).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Newton's rings: D₅ = 0.336 cm, D₁₅ = 0.590 cm, R = 100 cm. λ = (0.590² − 0.336²)/(4 × 10 × 100) = (0.3481 − 0.1129)/4000 = 5.88×10⁻⁵ cm = 588 nm.

**Example 2.** Anti-reflection MgF₂ (μ = 1.38) for 550 nm: t = λ/(4μ) = 550/(5.52) ≈ 99.6 nm.

**Example 3.** Liquid between lens and plate: D₁₀ changes from 1.40 cm to 1.27 cm ⇒ μ = (1.40/1.27)² ≈ 1.22.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the extra λ/2 on reflection at the denser surface.
- Using radius instead of diameter in Dₙ² formulas.
- Using r instead of the refraction angle in 2μt cos r.

activity.prompt: Newton's rings with a liquid: D(air) = 0.50 cm, D(liquid) = 0.40 cm for the same ring. μ = (Dair/Dliquid)²?

quiz.q: Centre of Newton's rings in reflected light is
quiz.why: At the centre of Newton's rings the air film thickness is zero, but reflection at the glass plate gives a λ/2 phase change, so the centre is dark.

quiz.q: Dₙ² for dark rings is proportional to
quiz.why: For dark rings Dₙ² = 4nλR, so Dₙ² is proportional to n.
An anti-reflection coating has optical thickness λ/4, so its actual thickness is λ/(4μ). Waves reflected from its two surfaces then cancel.
With a liquid of index μ the wavelength becomes λ/μ, so D² ∝ 1/μ and the rings contract.
For a wedge film the fringe width is β = λ/(2μθ).

scenes.text: A CD splits white light into colours.
Its tracks act as a reflection grating with ~625 lines per mm.

steps.title: Fraunhofer single slit (width a)
steps.body: Minima: a sin θ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2…). Central maximum angular half-width θ ≈ λ/a; linear width on screen 2λD/a. Intensity I = I₀(sin α/α)², α = πa sin θ/λ.

steps.title: Diffraction grating
steps.body:
(a + b) sin θ = nλ, where a + b = 1/N (N lines per unit length). Maximum order n_max < (a + b)/λ.
Resolving power R = λ/dλ = nN_total. Rayleigh criterion: two lines just resolved when the maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Slit a = 0.2 mm, λ = 600 nm, D = 2 m: central max width = 2λD/a = 2(600×10⁻⁹)(2)/(0.2×10⁻³) = 12 mm.

**Example 2.** Grating 5000 lines/cm, λ = 589 nm: a + b = 2×10⁻⁶ m. sin θ₁ = 0.2945 ⇒ θ₁ ≈ 17.1°. n_max = 2×10⁻⁶/589×10⁻⁹ = 3.4 ⇒ 3 orders.

**Example 3.** To resolve sodium D lines (589.0, 589.6 nm) in first order: N = λ/dλ ≈ 589.3/0.6 ≈ 982 lines needed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the grating formula for minima of a single slit (and vice versa).
- Forgetting to convert lines/cm to grating element in metres.
- Rounding n_max up instead of down.

activity.prompt: Match the formula

quiz.q: Narrowing the slit makes the central maximum
quiz.why: The central maximum has width ∝ λ/a, so narrowing the slit (smaller a) makes the diffraction pattern wider.
4000 lines/cm = 4 × 10⁵ lines/m, so the grating element is 1/(4 × 10⁵) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

quiz.q: Resolving power of grating depends on
quiz.why: The resolving power of a grating is R = nN, where n is the order and N the total number of lines illuminated.

quiz.q: Rayleigh criterion places max of one on
quiz.why: By Rayleigh's criterion, two sources are just resolved when the maximum of one falls on the first minimum of the other.

quiz.q: Max order for a + b = 1.5 µm, λ = 500 nm
quiz.why: (a + b) sin θ = nλ gives n = 1.5/0.5 = 3 at θ = 90°, which cannot be observed, so the highest observable order is 2.

scenes.text: Glare from a wet road is mostly horizontally polarised.
Polaroid glasses with a vertical transmission axis cut it out.

steps.title: Polarisation basics
steps.body:
Light is a transverse wave; polarisation fixes the direction of E. Methods: reflection, refraction (pile of plates), double refraction (calcite), selective absorption (polaroid), scattering.
**Malus' law:** I = I₀cos²θ. Unpolarised light through one polariser: I = I₀/2.
**Brewster's law:** tan θ_B = μ; reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular; reflected light is completely polarised.

steps.title: Double refraction and wave plates
steps.body: Calcite splits light into O-ray (obeys Snell) and E-ray (does not). Quarter-wave plate thickness t = λ/[4(μₑ − μₒ)] converts plane to circular/elliptical light; half-wave plate t = λ/[2(μₑ − μₒ)] rotates the plane of polarisation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Unpolarised I₀ through two polarisers at 60°: I = (I₀/2)cos²60° = I₀/8.

**Example 2.** Brewster angle for glass μ = 1.5: θ_B = tan⁻¹1.5 ≈ 56.3°; refraction angle = 90° − 56.3° = 33.7°.

**Example 3.** Quarter-wave plate of quartz (μₑ − μₒ = 0.009) for 590 nm: t = 590×10⁻⁹/(4 × 0.009) ≈ 16.4 µm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Malus' law to unpolarised light directly (first halve it).
- Using sin instead of tan in Brewster's law.
- Confusing quarter-wave and half-wave plate thickness.

activity.label: Angle between polariser and analyser (Malus' law)

quiz.why: Malus' law states that polarised light through an analyser at angle θ has intensity I = I₀cos²θ.
At the Brewster angle, tan θ_B = μ.

quiz.q: At Brewster angle reflected and refracted rays are
quiz.why: At the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are at 90° to each other (θ_B + r = 90°).

quiz.q: Unpolarised I₀ through one ideal polariser
quiz.why: An ideal polariser passes half of the intensity of unpolarised light (the average of cos²θ over all angles is 1/2), so I₀/2.
Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation proves that light is a transverse wave.

questions.q: Fringe width in YDSE is proportional to
questions.why: β = λD/d, so the fringe width is directly proportional to wavelength.

questions.q: Polaroids work by
questions.why: Polaroids work by selective absorption (dichroism): they absorb light vibrating in one direction and pass the perpendicular one.

questions.q: Interference requires
questions.why: Sustained interference requires coherent sources with a constant phase difference.

questions.q: Brewster angle for μ = √3
questions.why: tan θ_B = μ = √3, so θ_B = 60°.

questions.q: Grating with 6000 lines/cm, first-order angle for 500 nm: sin θ =
Three polarisers 0°, 45°, 90°; unpolarised I₀ in. Output
questions.why: The first polariser passes I₀/2. The 45° polariser passes (I₀/2)cos²45° = I₀/4, and the last (at 45° to the second) passes I₀/4 × 1/2 = I₀/8.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Newton's rings formed by reflected light have a dark centre.  Reason (R): At the contact point the air film thickness is zero and reflection at the glass plate adds a λ/2 phase change.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: at the contact point the film thickness is zero, but reflection from the glass plate adds a λ/2 phase change, giving an effective path difference of λ/2 (destructive), so the centre is dark.

questions.q: Single slit first minimum at 30° for λ = 600 nm. Slit width
questions.why: For a single slit the first minimum satisfies a sin θ = λ. a = 600 nm/sin 30° = 1200 nm = 1.2 μm.

questions.q: Newton's rings: D₄ = 0.30 cm, D₁₂ = 0.50 cm, R = 100 cm. λ ≈
questions.why: Dₙ² = 4nλR, so D₁₂² − D₄² = 4(12 − 4)λR. (0.25 − 0.09) = 32 × 100 λ, giving λ = 5 × 10⁻⁵ cm = 500 nm.

questions.q: Case: An oil film (μ = 1.25) on water looks green (λ = 500 nm) at normal incidence in reflection, first order bright. Minimum thickness
questions.why: Both reflections (air–oil and oil–water, since 1.33 > 1.25) have a π shift, which cancel: bright when 2μt = λ ⇒ t = 500/(2 × 1.25) = 200 nm.

questions.q: Lines needed to resolve 600.0 and 600.3 nm in 2nd order
questions.why: To resolve the doublet we need R = λ/Δλ = 600/0.3 = 2000 = nN. For n = 2, N = 1000 lines.

questions.q: Half-wave plate for 600 nm with μₑ − μₒ = 0.01 has thickness
questions.why: For a half-wave plate (μₑ − μₒ)t = λ/2, so t = 600 nm/(2 × 0.01) = 30 μm.

questions.q: Intensity ratio of maxima to minima if amplitudes are 3:1
YDSE in water (μ = 4/3): fringe width becomes
questions.why: In water the wavelength is λ/μ, so β = λD/(μd) = β_air × 3/4.

questions.q: Maximum order for grating 5000 lines/cm at λ = 700 nm
questions.why: 5000 lines/cm gives (a + b) = 2 μm. The maximum order is 2/0.7 = 2.86, so the integer part is 2.

courses.title: Engineering Physics · Unit 2 · Lasers and fibre optics
courses.summary: Absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission, Einstein coefficients, population inversion, He–Ne, ruby, Nd:YAG, CO₂ and semiconductor lasers, and optical fibres: total internal reflection, numerical aperture, modes, attenuation and dispersion.
outcomes: Explain stimulated emission, population inversion and pumping
Describe common lasers and their applications
Calculate numerical aperture, acceptance angle and V-number
Compute attenuation and explain dispersion in fibres
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

story.title: Why a laser beam is special

scenes.text: A laser pointer's red dot stays small across a hall; a torch beam spreads.
The secret is stimulated emission: photons cloning themselves in phase.

steps.title: Three processes
steps.body:
- **Absorption:** rate B₁₂N₁ρ(ν).
- **Spontaneous emission:** rate A₂₁N₂ — random phase/direction.
- **Stimulated emission:** rate B₂₁N₂ρ(ν) — emitted photon identical (same frequency, phase, direction, polarisation).
At equilibrium: B₁₂ = B₂₁ and A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³.

steps.title: Population inversion and pumping
steps.body:
Normally N₂ < N₁ (Boltzmann N₂/N₁ = e^(−hν/kT)). Lasing needs N₂ > N₁ (inversion) in a **metastable** state (lifetime ~ms versus ~ns). Pumping: optical (ruby), electrical discharge (He–Ne, CO₂), injection current (diodes).
Three-level vs four-level systems: four-level lasers need much less pumping because the lower laser level empties quickly.
Optical resonator: two mirrors (one partly transmitting) give feedback; L = mλ/2.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Ratio N₂/N₁ at 300 K for λ = 632.8 nm: hν = hc/λ = 3.14×10⁻¹⁹ J; kT = 4.14×10⁻²¹ J; ratio = e^(−75.9) ≈ 10⁻³³ — thermal excitation can never give inversion.

**Example 2.** Photon energy of a 1064 nm Nd:YAG laser: E = 1240/1064 ≈ 1.17 eV.

**Example 3.** A 5 mW He–Ne laser at 632.8 nm emits P/(hν) = 5×10⁻³/3.14×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.6×10¹⁶ photons/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying spontaneous emission produces the laser beam (it seeds it; stimulated emission amplifies).
- Forgetting the metastable level's role.
- Using E = hc/λ with λ in nm and h in J·s without converting.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Photon identical to the incident one

quiz.why: Laser light is coherent, almost monochromatic and highly directional.
Population inversion means more atoms are in the higher energy level than in the lower, N₂ > N₁, which is needed for laser action.
The Einstein coefficients are related by A₂₁/B₂₁ = 8πhν³/c³.
A four-level laser empties its lower laser level quickly, so population inversion is easy and it needs less pumping than a three-level laser.

scenes.text: Eye surgeons reshape the cornea with an excimer laser.
Factories cut steel with CO₂ lasers; fibres carry internet on diode lasers.

steps.title: Common lasers
steps.body:
- **Ruby** (Cr³⁺ in Al₂O₃): solid, 3-level, optical pumping by flash lamp, 694.3 nm, pulsed.
- **He–Ne:** gas, 4-level; He atoms excited by discharge transfer energy to Ne by resonant collisions; 632.8 nm, continuous.
- **Nd:YAG:** solid, 4-level, 1064 nm — cutting, welding, medicine.
- **CO₂:** molecular gas (vibrational levels), 10.6 µm, high power — cutting and welding.
- **Semiconductor (diode):** p–n junction, forward bias injects carriers; λ ≈ hc/E_g (e.g. GaAs ≈ 870 nm).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Band gap for a diode laser emitting 1550 nm: E_g = 1240/1550 = 0.80 eV.

**Example 2.** Coherence length of a source with Δλ = 0.01 nm at 600 nm: l = λ²/Δλ = 3.6×10⁻¹³/10⁻¹¹ = 3.6 cm.

**Example 3.** Beam divergence of a 2 mm aperture at 632.8 nm: θ ≈ λ/d ≈ 3.2×10⁻⁴ rad — the spot grows only ~3 cm over 100 m.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Fibre communication, barcode scanners, LiDAR, holography, laser printers, material processing, LASIK, dermatology, range finding and metrology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling ruby a four-level laser (it is three-level).
- Thinking He atoms lase in a He–Ne laser (Ne does).
- Never look into a laser beam — even milliwatt beams can damage the retina.

activity.prompt: Classify the laser

quiz.why: The He–Ne laser's well-known red line is at 632.8 nm.
The ruby laser (Cr³⁺ in Al₂O₃) is a three-level laser, so its lower level is the ground state.
The CO₂ laser works on vibrational–rotational transitions and emits in the far infrared at about 10.6 μm.
In a semiconductor diode laser, the photon energy is approximately the band gap, since light is produced by electron–hole recombination.
In the He–Ne laser, helium atoms are excited and transfer energy to neon, and the neon atoms are the ones that emit the laser light.

lessons.title: Optical fibres: principle, NA and acceptance angle

scenes.text: Light entering one end of a glass fibre comes out the other end even if the fibre is coiled.
Total internal reflection traps it inside the core.

steps.title: Structure and principle
steps.body: Core (n₁) surrounded by cladding (n₂ < n₁), then a protective buffer. Light hitting the core–cladding boundary above the critical angle θ_c = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁) is totally internally reflected.

steps.title: Key formulas
steps.body:
- Numerical aperture NA = √(n₁² − n₂²) = n₀ sin θₐ (θₐ = acceptance angle)
- Fractional index change Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ ⇒ NA ≈ n₁√(2Δ)
- V-number V = (2πa/λ)NA (a = core radius). Single-mode if V < 2.405; number of modes ≈ V²/2 (step index).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing NA = n₁ − n₂.
- Using diameter in V-number (it uses radius).
- Forgetting n₀ (outside medium) when the fibre is in water.

activity.prompt: NA for n₁ = 1.48, n₂ = 1.46 (3 decimals)

quiz.q: TIR requires light to go from
quiz.why: Total internal reflection needs light to travel from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.
The numerical aperture of a fibre is NA = √(n₁² − n₂²).
A step-index fibre supports only one mode when its V-number is below 2.405.
The acceptance angle satisfies sin θₐ = NA, so a larger NA gives a larger acceptance angle.
The cladding has a slightly lower refractive index than the core, so that light is totally internally reflected at the boundary.

lessons.title: Types of fibres, attenuation and dispersion

scenes.text: Undersea cables carry terabits per second over thousands of kilometres.
Low loss at 1550 nm and controlled dispersion make that possible.

steps.title: Fibre types
steps.body:
- **Step-index multimode:** large core, many modes, high modal dispersion — short links.
- **Graded-index multimode:** core index falls parabolically; modes travel at nearly equal speeds — LANs.
- **Single-mode step-index:** tiny core (~8–10 µm), no modal dispersion — long-haul.

steps.title: Losses and dispersion
steps.body:
Attenuation α (dB/km) = (10/L) log₁₀(Pᵢ/Pₒ). Causes: absorption (impurities, OH⁻), Rayleigh scattering (∝ 1/λ⁴), bending losses. Low-loss windows near 850, 1310 and 1550 nm (≈ 0.2 dB/km at 1550).
Dispersion spreads pulses: intermodal (multimode), chromatic (material + waveguide), polarisation-mode.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 km link, input 1 mW, output 0.5 mW: α = (10/10)log₁₀2 = 0.30 dB/km.

**Example 2.** Loss budget: 50 km at 0.25 dB/km = 12.5 dB plus 4 splices × 0.1 dB = 0.4 dB ⇒ 12.9 dB. Launch 0 dBm ⇒ receive −12.9 dBm.

**Example 3.** Step-index modal delay per km: Δt ≈ Ln₁Δ/c = 1000 × 1.5 × 0.01/(3×10⁸) = 50 ns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using natural log in dB formulas.
- Thinking graded-index fibres are single-mode.
- Ignoring connector/splice losses in a link budget.

activity.prompt: Match fibre properties

quiz.why: Fibre attenuation is α = (10/L) log₁₀(P_in/P_out) in dB per km.
A single-mode fibre carries just one mode, so there is no intermodal dispersion.
3 dB means 10 log(P_in/P_out) = 3, so P_in/P_out ≈ 2: the output is half of the input.
In a graded-index fibre, rays that travel longer paths go faster in lower-index regions, so arrival times are equalised and modal dispersion is reduced.
Rayleigh scattering from microscopic density fluctuations is the main intrinsic scattering loss in silica fibre.

questions.q: LASER stands for
questions.why: LASER means Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
options: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation

questions.q: Fibre works on
questions.why: An optical fibre guides light by total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.

questions.q: Ruby laser wavelength
questions.why: The ruby laser emits deep red light at 694.3 nm.

questions.q: Metastable state lifetime is about
questions.why: A metastable state has a long lifetime (about 10⁻³ s), compared with about 10⁻⁸ s for ordinary excited states, which allows population inversion.

questions.q: Critical angle for n₁ = 1.5, n₂ = 1.45
NA for n₁ = 1.5, n₂ = 1.45
Assertion (A): Thermal excitation alone cannot produce population inversion.  Reason (R): In thermal equilibrium N₂/N₁ = e^(−hν/kT) < 1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: in thermal equilibrium the Boltzmann distribution gives N₂/N₁ = e^(−hν/kT) < 1, so heating alone cannot put more atoms in the upper level, and pumping is needed.

questions.q: Diode laser with E_g = 1.42 eV emits about
Fibre loss 0.5 dB/km over 20 km: output fraction
questions.why: Total loss = 0.5 × 20 = 10 dB. 10 dB corresponds to a power ratio of 10, so the output is 1/10 = 10% of the input.

questions.q: V-number for a = 4 µm, NA = 0.1, λ = 1.55 µm
questions.why: V = 2πa NA/λ = 2π × 4 × 0.1/1.55 ≈ 1.62. This is below 2.405, so it is single-mode.

questions.q: Case: A 1 mW laser at 1550 nm feeds 80 km of fibre (0.2 dB/km) with 2 connectors of 0.5 dB each. Received power
questions.why: Fibre loss = 80 × 0.2 = 16 dB. Connector loss = 2 × 0.5 = 1 dB. Total 17 dB. Launch power 1 mW = 0 dBm, so received power = −17 dBm.

questions.q: Acceptance angle in air for NA = 0.5
questions.why: sin θₐ = NA = 0.5, so θₐ = 30°.

questions.q: Coherence length for λ = 500 nm, Δλ = 0.05 nm
Approximate number of modes for V = 20 (step index)
questions.why: For a step-index fibre the number of modes is about V²/2 = 400/2 = 200.

questions.q: Photons per second from a 1 mW, 620 nm laser
questions.why: Photon energy = 1240/620 eV = 2 eV = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Photons per second = 10⁻³/3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.1 × 10¹⁵.

courses.summary: Failures of classical physics, blackbody radiation, photoelectric and Compton effects, de Broglie waves, Heisenberg uncertainty, wave function and Schrödinger's equations, particle in a box and tunnelling.
outcomes: Explain blackbody, photoelectric and Compton results
Compute de Broglie wavelengths and uncertainty limits
Write and interpret Schrödinger's equations and the wavefunction
