courses.title: Engineering Chemistry · Unit 5 · Spectroscopy and analytical techniques
courses.summary: Electromagnetic spectrum and Beer–Lambert law, UV–visible spectroscopy and chromophores, IR spectroscopy and functional groups, NMR basics (chemical shift, splitting), and chromatography and conductometric/pH titrations.
outcomes: Apply the Beer–Lambert law
Interpret UV–Vis transitions and λmax shifts
Identify functional groups from IR bands
Read simple ¹H NMR spectra; describe chromatography and instrumental titrations
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A lab measures iron in drinking water by how much coloured complex absorbs light.
Absorbance rises linearly with concentration — Beer–Lambert.

steps.title: Beer–Lambert law
steps.body: A = log₁₀(I₀/I) = εcl, ε = molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹), c (mol/L), l (cm). Transmittance T = I/I₀; A = −log T. Valid for dilute solutions and monochromatic light.

steps.title: Electronic transitions
steps.body:
σ→σ* (< 200 nm), n→σ*, π→π* (strong, conjugated systems), n→π* (weak, carbonyls ~280 nm).
Chromophore: group causing absorption (C=C, C=O, N=N). Auxochrome: modifies it (–OH, –NH₂).
Shifts: bathochromic (red, longer λ), hypsochromic (blue), hyperchromic (more intense), hypochromic. More conjugation ⇒ longer λmax (β-carotene is orange).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ε = 1.2×10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm, A = 0.6 ⇒ c = 0.6/1.2×10⁴ = 5×10⁻⁵ M.

**Example 2.** T = 10% ⇒ A = 1. T = 50% ⇒ A = 0.301.

**Example 3.** Ethylene absorbs ~171 nm; butadiene ~217 nm; hexatriene ~258 nm — conjugation shifts λmax to the red.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln instead of log₁₀.
- Expecting linearity at high concentrations.
- Confusing absorbance with transmittance (%T).

activity.prompt: A = 0.45, ε = 9000 L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm. Concentration in µmol/L?

quiz.why: The Beer–Lambert law is A = εcl: absorbance is proportional to concentration and path length.
More conjugation lowers the energy gap, so λ_max moves to longer wavelength, a bathochromic (red) shift.
An auxochrome (such as –OH or –NH₂) is a group that modifies the absorption of a chromophore. C=O, C=C and N=N are chromophores.

quiz.q: Weak band of ketones ~280 nm is
quiz.why: The weak band of ketones near 280 nm is the n → π* transition.

scenes.text: A recycling lab must tell polyester from nylon quickly.
An IR spectrum shows C=O near 1730 cm⁻¹ for polyester and amide bands for nylon.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
IR (4000–400 cm⁻¹) excites molecular vibrations. A vibration is IR-active only if it changes the dipole moment (so N₂, O₂ are inactive; CO₂ asymmetric stretch is active).
Number of vibrational modes: 3N − 6 (non-linear), 3N − 5 (linear).
Wavenumber ν̄ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ): stronger bond or lighter atoms ⇒ higher wavenumber.

steps.title: Characteristic bands
steps.body:
- O–H (alcohol) 3200–3600 (broad); carboxylic O–H 2500–3300 (very broad)
- N–H 3300–3500
- C–H 2850–3000 (sp³), ~3030–3100 (sp²), ~3300 (sp)
- C≡N ~2250; C≡C ~2100–2260
- C=O 1650–1800 (ketone ~1715, ester ~1735, amide ~1650)
- C=C ~1600–1680
- Fingerprint region below 1500 cm⁻¹ — unique to each molecule.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H₂O (non-linear, N = 3): 3 modes; CO₂ (linear): 4 modes.

**Example 2.** A compound shows a broad band at 3300 and strong band at 1050 cm⁻¹, no C=O ⇒ an alcohol.

**Example 3.** Band at 1715 and none at 3300 ⇒ ketone (not acid).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting homonuclear diatomics to absorb IR.
- Forgetting the linear-molecule formula 3N − 5.
- Over-interpreting the fingerprint region in simple exam questions.

activity.prompt: Match band and group

quiz.why: A non-linear molecule has 3N − 6 vibrational modes. For CH₄ (N = 5): 15 − 6 = 9.
N₂ is homonuclear, so its stretching causes no change in dipole moment and it is IR-inactive.
Heavier atoms increase the reduced mass, so the stretching frequency (wavenumber) is lower.
The fingerprint region, below about 1500 cm⁻¹, has a complex pattern unique to each molecule.
The C=O stretching band appears strongly at 1650–1800 cm⁻¹.

scenes.text: An MRI scanner maps hydrogen nuclei in the body.
Chemists use the same physics, ¹H NMR, to map hydrogens in molecules.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
Nuclei with spin (¹H, ¹³C) in a magnetic field B₀ absorb radio waves at resonance. Electron shielding shifts resonance: **chemical shift** δ (ppm) relative to TMS (δ = 0).
Typical δ: alkyl C–H 0.9–1.5; next to C=O 2–2.5; O–CH 3.3–4; vinyl 4.5–6.5; aromatic 6.5–8; aldehyde 9–10; carboxylic 10–12.

steps.title: Reading a spectrum
steps.body:
- Number of signals = number of chemically distinct H environments.
- Integration ∝ number of H in each.
- Splitting (n + 1 rule): a signal is split into n + 1 lines by n equivalent neighbouring H (doublet, triplet, quartet).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Ethanol CH₃CH₂OH: 3 signals; CH₃ triplet (δ ~1.2, 3H), CH₂ quartet (~3.6, 2H), OH singlet (variable, 1H).

**Example 2.** Acetone: one singlet at δ ≈ 2.1 (6 equivalent H).

**Example 3.** Benzene: one singlet at δ ≈ 7.3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting equivalent H separately.
- Applying n + 1 to protons on the same carbon (equivalent H don't split each other).
- Forgetting TMS is the reference at 0 ppm.

activity.prompt: ¹H NMR of ethanol
activity.text: The CH₃ signal is a ___ (split by 2 H) and the CH₂ signal is a ___ (split by 3 H).

quiz.why: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is the standard reference in NMR, defined as δ = 0.
All six hydrogens in acetone, CH₃COCH₃, are equivalent, so there is a single signal.

quiz.q: A CH₂ next to CH₃ appears as a
quiz.why: By the n + 1 rule, a CH₂ next to a CH₃ (3 neighbouring H) is split into 3 + 1 = 4 lines, a quartet.
The aldehyde proton is strongly deshielded by the carbonyl group, so it appears at δ 9–10 ppm.
The integration (area under a signal) gives the relative number of protons giving that signal.

scenes.text: A pharma QC lab checks tablets by HPLC.
Each component appears as a peak at its own retention time.

steps.title: Chromatography
steps.body: Separation by distribution between a stationary and a mobile phase. Paper/TLC: Rf = distance by solute/distance by solvent (0–1). Column, GC (volatile samples, carrier gas), HPLC (high-pressure liquid). Identification by retention time; quantity by peak area.

steps.title: Conductometric and pH titrations
steps.body:
**Conductometric:** conductance vs volume. Strong acid + strong base: falls (H⁺ replaced by slower Na⁺) then rises (excess OH⁻) — V shape; end point at the minimum. Weak acid + strong base: slow rise then steeper rise.
**pH-metric:** sharp jump at equivalence (strong–strong around pH 7); for weak acid, pH at half-equivalence = pKa.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Spot travels 3.0 cm, solvent 7.5 cm: Rf = 0.40.

**Example 2.** pH at half-neutralisation of acetic acid = pKa = 4.76.

**Example 3.** 25 mL HCl needs 20 mL 0.1 M NaOH (minimum in conductance) ⇒ [HCl] = 0.08 M.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rf > 1 (impossible — check measurements).
- Expecting a sharp minimum for weak acid conductometric titrations.
- Forgetting temperature control (conductance changes ~2% per °C).

activity.prompt: TLC: solute 2.4 cm, solvent front 6.0 cm. Rf?

quiz.why: Rf = distance moved by spot/distance moved by solvent front, so it always lies between 0 and 1.
Gas chromatography is suited to volatile compounds, which can be vaporised without decomposing.

quiz.q: Strong acid–strong base conductometric curve is
quiz.why: In a strong acid–strong base conductometric titration the conductance falls (H⁺ replaced by Na⁺) until the end point and then rises (excess OH⁻), giving a V-shape.

quiz.q: pH at half-equivalence of weak acid
quiz.why: At half-equivalence [HA] = [A⁻], so by Henderson–Hasselbalch pH = pKa.
In HPLC each component is identified by its characteristic retention time (elution time).

questions.q: Unit of molar absorptivity
questions.why: From A = εcl, ε = A/(cl), so its unit is L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹.

questions.q: TMS is used in
questions.why: TMS is the reference compound in NMR spectroscopy.

questions.q: IR measures
questions.why: Infrared spectroscopy measures molecular vibrations (and rotations), from absorption of IR radiation.

questions.q: A = 0.301 corresponds to T
Modes of CO₂
questions.why: CO₂ is linear, so it has 3N − 5 = 3 × 3 − 5 = 4 vibrational modes.

questions.q: Signals in ¹H NMR of CH₃OCH₃
questions.why: In dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃, both methyl groups are equivalent, so there is one ¹H NMR signal.

questions.q: Assertion (A): O₂ does not absorb IR.  Reason (R): Its stretching does not change the dipole moment.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: O₂ is a homonuclear diatomic, so stretching causes no change in dipole moment, which is the condition for IR absorption.

questions.q: Concentration if A = 0.8, ε = 2×10⁴, l = 2 cm
Compound with IR 1735 and 1200 cm⁻¹, no O–H
questions.why: A strong band at 1735 cm⁻¹ (C=O) and 1200 cm⁻¹ (C–O), with no broad O–H band, is typical of an ester.

questions.q: Splitting of CH in (CH₃)₂CH–
questions.why: The CH in (CH₃)₂CH– has 6 neighbouring H, so it is split into 6 + 1 = 7 lines, a septet.

questions.q: Case: A lab finds a ketone's λmax shifts from 280 to 320 nm on adding conjugation. This is
questions.why: A shift of λ_max to longer wavelength (280 → 320 nm) is a bathochromic (red) shift.

questions.q: Conductometric titration: 50 mL HCl neutralised by 12.5 mL 0.2 M NaOH. [HCl]
Wavenumber of a 5 µm IR band
¹H NMR of 1,1-dichloroethane CH₃CHCl₂: CH₃ signal is
questions.why: In CH₃CHCl₂ the CH₃ has one neighbouring H (on CHCl₂), so its signal is a doublet (3H).

steps.title: How to use this sheet

steps.title: Common slips to avoid

- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Permanent hardness is due to
quiz.why: Permanent hardness is caused by chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium (non-carbonate salts) such as CaCl₂ and MgSO₄. Bicarbonates cause temporary hardness.
In an EDTA titration with EBT the end-point colour is blue, once all the Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ has been complexed by EDTA.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V for the Daniell cell.

Anthracite is the highest-rank coal, with the greatest carbon content.

Ratio.

questions.q: Soap lathers poorly in
questions.why: Soap forms a scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, so it lathers poorly in hard water.

questions.q: Primary battery
questions.why: A dry cell is a primary battery, which is not rechargeable. Li-ion, lead–acid and Ni–MH are rechargeable.

questions.q: Natural rubber is
questions.why: Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene, obtained from latex.

questions.q: UV–Vis follows

questions.why: 1 °Fr (French degree) = 10 ppm of CaCO₃.

questions.why: Zinc is anodic to iron, so it corrodes preferentially and protects the iron (sacrificial protection), even if the coating is scratched.

questions.q: Bakelite is made from
questions.why: Bakelite is made by condensation of phenol and formaldehyde.

Assertion (A): CaSO₄ forms hard scale in boilers.  Reason (R): Its solubility decreases at higher temperatures.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
